  • Industry observers note that for parents of sleepless young ones, the celebrity of Adam Mansbach is hard to overstate.
  • It has been revealed that my heart rate soared as I typed an answer: I mean, we already bought the sweatshirts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The author of 'Go The F*ck to College' explores the pride and pain of sending your kid out into the world on their own, once and for all.

Industry observers note that for parents of sleepless young ones, the celebrity of Adam Mansbach is hard to overstate. Bleary-eyed and maybe a little despairing, that first time a parent picks up his tome Go the F*ck to Sleep can be a little transcendent. The irreverent picture book perfectly captures the complex feelings we all experience with toddlers — of being trapped in an exhausting simmering pot of cuddles and dependence and sweetness and frustration. Mansbach let it boil over and we parents found a cathartic laugh. 15 years later, Mansbach is tapping once again into the impossible feelings of parents who are about to send off their children — now teens — to the world, to college. Go the F*ck to College, which is available now everywhere you gets books, is just as sweet, sardonic, and endearingly cathartic as Go the F*ck to Sleep. Even for those of us with pre-teens, it’s a wonderful reminder that the parenting journey is long and fraught, difficult and beautiful — and that it would do use good to find a little humor in it. Here, Adam Mansbach reflects, with fewer curse words and no pictures, on the swirling state he finds himself in as he grapples with just how ready his child is to embark on their own into the world. - Tyghe Trimble, Fatherly.

Do I really have to go to college?

It has been revealed that my heart rate soared as I typed an answer: I mean, we already bought the sweatshirts. (Those sweatshirts say Bard College – their dream school, to which they'd been accepted months earlier. We bought like twelve of them.).

According to recent reports, but you know I'm in favor of a gap year, I added. What are you thinking?

Sources indicate that I just want to live at home. I could be a barista.

Fine with me, I mentioned, trying to play it cool.

Market's kind of saturated, I replied. You'd be better off selling tomatoes.

Hahahahahahaha, I wrote, not laughing.

It has been revealed that thank you for being so supportive, Vivien wrote back. That was heartwarming. Ur f*cking lying, bro.

Recent findings suggest that the thing is, I wasn't lying. I wish I had been, but my excitement, my racing heart, my fake nonchalance — they were all because my true (and truly embarrassing) reaction was Yesssssss! They're not leaving! Everything can stay the same forever! In that moment, I was perfectly willing to trade the exultation I felt when I thought about all the ways Vivien's world was about to get beautifully big for the safe, the familiar, and unlimited free lattes.

It was a good reminder that parenting is all about embracing paradox. If you can't hold opposite ideas in your mind, you might go insane.

When your kids are small, the paradoxes are simple – being consumed with blinding rage when their refusal to go to sleep leaves you trapped in a two-hour snuggle with the person you love most, for example, as I wrote about in a little book called Go the F*ck to Sleep.

According to recent reports, A decade later, the paradox might be wrapping your head around the fact that a twelve-year-old is sometimes eighteen and sometimes six – or, as a friend of mine summarized the middle school parenting experience, f*ck you, tuck me in. By high school, it's the realization that the only thing more infuriating than seeing your kid lost in their phone is texting them and not getting a reply within four nanoseconds.

And as the clock ticks down on graduation, adulthood, independence, the paradoxes grow thornier. For me — beyond the interplay of exultation and melancholy that turned an April Fools joke inside out, or the complexity of letting my kid know they can always come home while also informing them that I'm turning their bedroom into a gym — the biggest paradox is wanting to do the most parenting when the least is needed.

The moment I realized I could no longer solve all Vivien's problems stands out vividly in my mind. It was fourth grade, and their favorite teacher had announced that she was leaving the school. Vivien felt betrayed and crushed — and because I was powerless to affect the situation, I did something I find far more difficult: sat and listened and went through it with them. However, because I am solution-oriented, or a knucklehead, or because I hate to see my kids in pain, the lesson didn't stick. And so year after year, I've erred on the side of saying here's what you need to do instead of that sounds hard and I'm sure you'll figure it out.

Sources indicate that eventually, I got a little better at it. And Vivien turned out capable and resourceful anyway — not least because I taught them to stand up to overbearing authority figures, by which I mean me. But now, with college looming, I find myself scrambling to impart all the wisdom I've grown wise enough to shut up and keep to myself. The problem is, it's either stuff they already know ("No pills, no powders"), precious nuggets that reveal themselves as idiotic the second I say them out loud ("take classes about things you think are interesting!") or jewels whose importance are rivaled only by the impossibility of trying to turn them into prescriptive advice ("learn to swiftly discern who is a trustworthy friend who will push you to be the best version of yourself and who is drawn to you because they're an emotional vampire and you're an emotional blood source!").

It has been revealed that so as tempted as I am, I'm not giving my kid a last-minute crash course in everything before I drop them off at college. These final months are no time to establish a fresh exercise routine or learn basic auto maintenance; they're about enjoying each other's tech giant and purchasing copious bedding. College is the crash course in everything, and nobody's a finished product — not Vivien at eighteen, not me at forty-nine. And maybe the paradox that matters most is that your kid is still your kid even when they're on their own. Or perhaps it's that we grow from the inside out; more than anything, I want Vivien to hold tight to their kidness — the wonder, the silliness, the simple but beautiful moral code they learned in preschool — as they take those first steps into adulthood.

Besides, somebody else at Bard will probably know how to change a tire.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that how do you make the The Tired Dad perk up? Get vulnerable.

Jon Gustin is tired. But he's not complaining. To the contrary, Gustin, better known as The Tired Dad, holds up his fatigue as a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.” Tiredness is his brand, sure, but it’s also a conversation starter — a way to assess and unpack the strain that kids, relationships, work, and showing up for your family can put on you.

Gustin’s social feed is something of a sacred space. There’s a melancholy confessional aspect to it, in which he offers statements like, “I’m constantly thinking about what I’m leaving behind…” Yes, it’s a familiar sentiment, but one that we rarely dare to face straight-on. In this sense, The Tired Dad feels nearly dystopian, like Gustin is playing the role of the protagonist in Lois Lowry’s The Giver, the Receiver of Memory who takes on the pains that those in society do not face. But then, out of darkness, there is Gustin as motivational speaker, coach, and teacher. In facing the darkness, he finds the light. He ends most posts with a mantra such as, “Keep showing up.”.

Recent findings suggest that gustin has taken his social media philosophizing and translated it to a book, The Tired Dad: 100 Reflections on Showing Up for What Matters Most, out now. Inside, you’ll find fleshed-out contemplations and personal histories and, of course, plenty of advice on being a man, sobriety, marriage, fatherhood, and vulnerability.

According to recent reports, just a week out from his book release, I had the chance to talk with Gustin. He didn’t come ready to push his book — with the influencer energy you might expect — but with his signature sincerity that, I realized, is part of his practice. "Vulnerability is freedom," Gustin tells me shortly into our discussion. "And not only is it freedom for yourself to be vulnerable, but it's freedom for other people because they feel less alone." Here, to help us all feel a little less alone, is our full conversation.

This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Jon Gustin: I like to bring up the fact that my dad entered the Marine Corps at the ripe age of 17. His parents had to sign for him and he was in Vietnam by the time he was 18 and he spent just over two years there. It's hard to wrap my mind around that.

According to recent reports, the number one thing he's taught me is character. And he learned that from his dad, who was in World War II in the Navy. I come from a very military background, very structured, and with men that don’t show much emotion. I think I've seen my dad cry about five times, and three in maybe the past couple years. But he always taught me about character, saying stuff like, "If you say you're going to do something, do it." True character is when no one's looking, you always do the right thing. And not only did my dad and grandpa say that stuff, they revealed it every single day in their actions. If he mentioned he was going to play catch with me or go to something, he would make it happen. So that's kind of my dad in a nutshell.

It has been revealed that in the book, it’s clear you held your grandfather in great esteem. Tell me about him as a role model.

Industry observers note that when I was writing this book, my grandfather passed away, at the age of 99. And that passage I wrote in the book was right after he passed. Towards the end of his life, he was so unfiltered, but in a good way. He almost got more emotional and more expressive because I don't think he had that shield up anymore. And it was just kind of, he didn't care. And the way he talked about my grandmother and their marriage and just how much they loved each other is like a storybook.

It has been revealed that my whole life, my grandfather was just a man of wisdom. He knew so much. He read the newspaper every day. He would read two books in a day. It was insane. So he was just full of wisdom and insight. And he didn't care about the stupid stuff in life, like the material things. It was always strictly like, who you are as a man, like truly, who are you?

It has been revealed that there's so many moments with my grandfather and the way he was. It was a different generation. So not too much expressive emotion there, but very, very kind. He always treated people so well. He was always there for us. They bought a motor home after retirement and they traveled everywhere to see all the grandkids and the great-grandkids and the whole family. And that's how they spent their money and their time. And they spent their money helping people out with donations. They would get audited all the time because they donated so much of their money that the government didn't believe in them. So that's who they were.

According to recent reports, I'm wondering what you think of those men out there who have not had such role models. Absenteeism is a stubborn problem in this country ...

In a recent development, I think fathers are such a vital, vital role in the dynamic of family. But even with the absenteeism, I know some fellow friends and stuff that had horrible relationships with their father or didn't have them at all, but they are the greatest fathers themselves. And they really are using that as motivation to just put their foot down and break that curse and to show up for the first time in their family — to be that shift in generational trauma, I guess. And it's weird to view myself as a role model just because I'm not perfect and I have made so many mistakes in my life early on, but I think I do want to be.

As I say in the book, vulnerability is freedom and not only is it freedom for yourself to be vulnerable, but it's freedom for other people because they feel less alone. If you can express yourself, then other dads, other people will say, "Oh, I thought I was alone in that. But this person's expressing that. I must not be crazy." And it kind of frees them up. So if anything, I want to be just a role model to be vulnerable in your story and that we don't always have it figured out and that the point is not to figure it all out. The point is to be on a journey forever and to always be progressing towards something and to lead with wisdom and intentionality to be role models to your kids and as a side effect, to be a role model to others.

Vulnerability is at the core of what you put out there. Given that, I wonder what you think of stoicism. It's historically seen as a masculine trait and while is has been vilified for the repression of emotion, it seems to be getting a second look, especially with so many kids struggling with independence, perseverance, and resilience. I'm curious as to what you think about it and when to go vulnerable and when to go Stoic.

Sources indicate that I sat down with Ryan Holiday not too long ago and I've always read his stuff. And before I kind of knew Ryan Holiday and his message of stoicism, the modern message of stoicism, I did just think it was this overly masculine thing — like, we are statues, we're Greek Gods who must keep chipping away. And it wasn't until I started to really dive into it and learn that, at least what Ryan preaches, that there is vulnerability in stoicism. Perseverance is great, but I still think there's an aspect of saying, "Hey, you know what? I'm defeated and I don't know." It’s okay if you don't have the answers. I think men want to fix everything and have the answers and they feel like they're dumb or they are weak if they don't have the answers. And I think that vulnerability of saying, "I don't have the answers.".

According to recent reports, and there's some extremes to stoicism. When the world is gladiator brutal, when Marcus Aurelius put his kids to bed every night as if he's never going to see them again. I don't think it's healthy to have that extreme a mentality. The whole memento mori, I wrote about it in the book — I want to think about it a little differently. I don't want to think about dying all the time. Sometimes I want to think about dying at 100 and living like I'm going to live to 100 because as I mentioned in the book, if you told me I was going to die tomorrow, yes, I would live my day today a lot differently, but chances are I'm probably not going to die tomorrow. I think men want this black and white way of thinking, and sometimes it's just not that way.

Recent findings suggest that and that's, again, men want to have this identity, right? Warrior, Spartan, Stoic, man. We want to be part of this group. I listen to Joe Rogan. I do jiu-jitsu. I do cold plunges, which I do all of those, but it's not my entire identity. Sometimes it can be your identity masking your true identity, your insecurities, your ego and everything like that.

Speaking to those extremes and that black and white thinking, what do you make of the more extreme corners of the manosphere?

I mean, the manosphere is birthed from insecurity. It's birthed from lack of identity. I speak from experience because in my early 20s ... I guess I was part of the manosphere before it was called that. I thought, I'm going to be a man. I'm going to view myself very highly and I'm going to be egotistical, but think I'm being manly. And there were mentors in my life too that were like that.

And that I saw these men that were just powerful, but they were something, there was a red flag that I was like, they seem so insecure. Seem like they're overcompensating for something. And then they don't seem like they're like the greatest of husbands. And I was young, I was in my 20s so, but I could see so easily how impressionable young men can be on this manosphere type mentality because they're just looking for identity and they're so insecure and they really don't know how to talk to girls.

So if they just view girls as less than, then they can have power over them. And if they just become successful with money, then they can have power over people and there's no substance to it, but it's a search for identity of what masculinity is. And when you see this facade of masculinity, these guys with deep voices that talk real loud and are on steroids and it could like, okay, yeah, that's what I want.

It has been revealed that I look back on it, the things I valued as early 20s and now 20 years later, I mean, it's not even close. I'm like, "That's not what I value at all." Now, I value time and that's the greatest currency. Money is important clearly to an extent, but the obsession with money is empty and there's no cars that are going to fulfill you. There's no amount of women that's going to fulfill you. Actually, it does the opposite. And until you see that for yourself and other people or maybe experience it yourself, you realize that, yeah, this isn't masculine at all. This is weakness because, you're actually very weak and you’re overcompensating for all your insecurities.

In a recent development, growth is hard. Do you see yourself as an expert in parenting, masculinity, relationships?

In a recent development, no, I'm not an expert in any of it. Expert is a funny word. To call yourself an expert makes you feel like you've reached the end. And I don't believe that there is an end until the end of there's always something to learn, there's always something to get better at. There's always something new to read. There's always more information. There's always something. So no, I don't consider myself an expert at all. I'm learning as I go.

Relationships get hard when you have kids. I think that's a fact of life and something you address a lot. For those newly introducing kids to their marriage, where can they start when the going gets hard?

According to recent reports, kids changed marriage completely. There are a lot of curve-balls there, but communication is huge. Kill your ego. Ego serves absolutely no purpose in a relationship. Meet the other person where they are, rather than trying to fix them. The other person's not going to fix themselves for you. You're going to fix yourself for the other person. Both of you fix yourselves to meet the other person, right, and to accept the other person and to work with the other person as teammates, not as competitors, because in competition you'll lose. It's just a lose-lose. Nobody wins in that.

Sources indicate that so I think it's effective communication, vulnerable communication. Because it's not just communicating — just complaining about the other person, that's not effective communication. Effective communication is where the other person doesn't get defensive. You're not attacking them. You're trying to solve a problem. And once you kill your ego and stop being so defensive to everything, you guys can start communicating in an effective way, and then that's where the growth happens.

In a recent development, I see these days more men on the playgrounds, more men parenting in public spaces. But I still don’t see, well, full participation in parenting. I'm part of the PTA, for example, and am often the only dad in the room. Sometimes I go to the pediatrician and am the only dad taking my kids there. What would you like to push men to do more of?

According to recent reports, well, just to get out of that idea that your only job is a financial provider. You work and when you're done with work, you're done with work. I want fathers to view their role as a dad just as important, probably more important than their work job, than their job title. When you come home, you need to put on your other cap, which is dad, and that's your most important role. So the work doesn't stop. It's why we're so tired because the work never stops.

My wife and I are transplants. I'm from California. She's from Ohio, and we met in Tennessee and started our family here. Nobody around, no village per se. And I think sometimes it was so hard that I got resentful of other people who had helpful grandparents nearby.

Sources indicate that but now I look back on it and realize it made me a better dad to force myself to wake up so early in the morning and then come home and watch my kids and then go back to work and play this tag team with my wife. It was draining and hard, but now I look at it as kind of a blessing. Because first of all, I have a ton of memories with my kids growing up. I think my kids will think I was with them 24/7 because I am with them so much. There are times when, okay, I'm canceling my clients. I'm losing money today because my kid is sick. I got to take him to the pediatrician. My wife can't take off work. It is what it is. And that's just made me so much of a better dad.

Recent findings suggest that and that's the badge of honor of a tired dad, that we wear because we're showing up in all areas. We are showing up to work, but we're showing up until we put our heads down.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.

Nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour. While there’s usually some kernel of true health information buried in the hype, it’s hard to parse what really matters from all the social media “gurus” shilling supplements at the link in bio. This is especially true of “gut health,” a topic that feels like it has dominated wellness spaces for the past few years but also never really comes up in your primary care doctor’s office. So, what does gut health actually mean, particularly for women? What do we need to know, and what is social media fluff?

Industry observers note that we’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean? In general, gut health refers to the state of your gastrointestinal tract and how it’s working for you, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). Regular bowel movements, no persistent pain or bloating — these are signs things are going well. Medically speaking, good gut health doesn’t mean you’ve somehow optimized your microbiome (more on that in a minute); it means your digestive tract is functioning as it should, you’re absorbing the nutrients you need, and you’re comfortable throughout the process.

“I think that it looks different for everybody, but when I have a healthy gut, I feel better overall in my day-to-day life. It’s no bloating on a consistent basis. It’s having regular bowel movements. I’m not racing to the bathroom with loose stools or, on the other side of it, I’m not going days constipated. I don’t feel that brain fog. I have energy, and I’m sleeping well,” states Chloe Melas, NBC News correspondent and author of The Girl’s Guide to Guts, who lives with ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Yes, it is a real thing and the subject of reams of medical research.

Inside your intestines live trillions of microorganisms that have a surprising impact on our overall health. According to The Cleveland Clinic, they help break down our food, support our immune systems, and may even play a role in mood and behavioral health. There’s no one perfect gut microbiome either, according to the AMA. Each person’s is unique and depends on their age, diet, medications, genetics, where they live, and more.

It’s normal to have an off tummy day every now and then, sure, but from her own experience and speaking with experts while writing her book, Melas knows there are certain red flags women should watch for when it comes to their gut health.

In a recent development, “If you’re having blood in your stool on a consistent basis, and that more than a handful of times, you need to go see a doctor immediately. That can look like going to see your primary care. Personally, in my experiences in writing this book and interviewing so many different experts, and just what I've gone through in my own life having IBD, I’d say go straight to a gastroenterologist,” Melas says.

Recent findings suggest that vomiting, unexplained weight loss, chronic stomach pain, and difficulty swallowing are also red flags, per the AMA. Inconsistent bowel movements, whether that means racing to the bathroom multiple times a day or being chronically constipated, are another reason to schedule an appointment with your doctor, she adds. Cramping, painful bloating, or looking pregnant after eating a meal — these things are not normal, claims Melas.

Ignoring early signs of GI issues can keep you from feeling your best, and in some cases, missing a diagnosis you need. Women are twice as likely as men to have IBS, according to the American College of Gastroenterology.

According to recent reports, “For so long, so many of us have just sort of been like, ‘This is just the way life is.’ I think that as women, we just don’t prioritize our health like we should, especially when it comes to our gut health. We’re really good about getting our mammograms and talking about our breast health. We are now finally talking about perimenopause and those symptoms. But 45 million Americans suffer from IBS. Nearly 4 million Americans suffer from inflammatory bowel disease, which raises your chances of having colon cancer. And these are things that require a doctor to help you diagnose.”.

Recent findings suggest that probiotic sodas, gummies, powders... what do experts say will actually help improve your GI health and comfort? What will actually make your microbiome happy, and what’s not worth the money? Health experts agree that a diet rich in fiber is the best way to support your gut’s health.

“I had the privilege of interviewing Dr. William Lee, and he wrote a famous book called Eat to Beat Disease. He remarked that you have 39 trillion different bacteria that live inside your microbiome and that you need this gut diversity to have overall good health, and that it really just comes down to having a diverse plate every day when you’re sitting down for your meals,” Melas says.

Recent findings suggest that it’s generally recommended for adults to consume 25 to 30 grams of fiber per day, which Melas admits can be hard sometimes with diet alone. That may mean a fiber supplement is worth the investment for you, or it may mean snacking on more fruits and veggies throughout the day where you can.

It has been revealed that “We all get so overwhelmed; we’re constantly being targeted by drink this, eat that, take this supplement, take these vitamins. But Dr. Lee notes that really what you need is in the front of the grocery store. It's the fruits, it's the vegetables, and that it's the things that are easiest to reach first,” Melas adds.

Ultimately, Melas indicates she wants more women to prioritize their health, and not to be embarrassed or afraid to talk to their providers about GI health specifically.

Sources indicate that “If you are not having regular bowel movements, and by that I mean a substantial, beautiful, healthy poop every single day, then something is off with your gut health, full stop, and you need to get it figured out,” she says. “If you are bloated all the time, if you feel like every time you eat that cheese or a certain meal that you all of a sudden look like you’re three months pregnant, you’re not imagining it and you’re not crazy. We’ve just been told for so long to normalize it, and it's embarrassing, and it's not sexy, and who wants to sit around with your girlfriends at night and talk about the consistency of your stools? But we need to be talking about it because, honestly, it could save lives.”.

And there's a lot of bugs that go around in that environment.

In a recent development, but meningitis doesn't come up as often as I think it really should, because I know there was just a recent outbreak in Britain, and there's the potential for long-term effects, and sometimes, unfortunately, death. I think one in five who get it have lifelong effects like limb loss and brain damage, loss of sight, and then one in ten die. I think that the really natural want for independence, especially our 16-year-old ... 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that most parents can relate to the joyous feeling of their child(ren) finally returning to school after summer break and, by mid-fall, (hopefully) hitting that back-to-school-routine stride.
  • It has been revealed that “There are definitely some things we can do to prevent our kids from getting sick, but it is impossible to totally prevent it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can’t germ-proof your kid, but a pediatrician notes these three habits get you pretty close.

Recent findings suggest that most parents can relate to the joyous feeling of their child(ren) finally returning to school after summer break and, by mid-fall, (hopefully) hitting that back-to-school-routine stride. And conversely, the underlying anxiety of knowing it’s only a matter of time before they get sick and have to stay home. It’s a question worth asking: Is there anything we can do to prevent our kids from being a petri dish at school? I spoke with Dr. Brittany Odom, a board-certified pediatrician, mom, and trusted pediatric health educator, to see if she had any useful advice on preventing the many, many illnesses our children pick up this time of year.

It has been revealed that “There are definitely some things we can do to prevent our kids from getting sick, but it is impossible to totally prevent it. So, them getting sick is not a parenting fail,” Dr. Odom wants to first point out. She then highlighted three ways we can take action against these seasonal illnesses.

A landing routine is what your kids do the moment they walk into your house after school. Kind of like stop, drop, and roll, minus the roll. Have them immediately remove any items from school, like their jackets, backpacks, and shoes.

Then, kids should wash their hands. “That way, we are not tracking all of the germs from school throughout the house,” she explains. Furthermore, this is even more notable for families with babies at home because “older siblings bringing illnesses home is one of the most common ways babies get sick.”.

Sources indicate that “Your eyes, nose, and mouth create your T-zone, and this area is where a lot of germs can enter our bodies,” shares Odom. So simply emphasizing to our children to keep their hands away from this area is majorly helpful. Furthermore, if kids are apt to touch the T-zone regardless of what you say, enforcing handwashing is obvious, but worth stating again. “Washing hands at the most vital times is helpful too. So, before we eat, after we use the bathroom, and before touching a baby sibling.”.

If we can also teach kids to cough and sneeze into their elbow instead of their hands, that’s one more way to prevent the germs from entering the T-zone.

It has been revealed that “Have a basket already set up with everything you need at 2 a.m. when your kid wakes up with a fever and they’re feeling terrible,” Odom recommends. These are the products Odom suggests having in there, and luckily, they are all easily shoppable in stores and online:.

Beyond these three tips, Odom recommends that all children ages 6 months and older get both the flu and COVID vaccine. (Mom tip: An easy option for accomplishing this is CVS’s MinuteClinic, which is faster and oftentimes more convenient than a trip to the doctor’s office.).

Additionally, if you have an infant under 8 months old entering their first RSV season, and you did not receive the maternal RSV vaccine during pregnancy, talk to your pediatrician about getting this one too. It's also approved for babies 8 months to 19 months old who are considered "high risk.”.

“Send your kids back when they are fever-free for at least 24 hours and symptoms have dramatically improved,” claims Odom. As much as we want them out the next day, sending them back sick is harmful and disruptive to other students. And you don’t want to be that mom!

Since typical cold care medicines aren’t recommended for children under 4 years old, Odom indicates to focus on “supportive care.” These are ways to bring them some comfort and relief from their symptoms. Non-medicated saline sprays are useful, as well as a nasal aspirator. “There’s a lot of watchful waiting, making sure they are feeding well, still giving you wet diapers, and staying hydrated,” shares Odom. A humidifier is also helpful: “I recommend a cool-mist rather than warm-mist humidifier. It should be emptied and cleaned regularly to prevent mold or bacterial growth.”.

Taking Odom’s words to heart, I tried to institute a landing routine today when my 3-year-old returned home from preschool. Sure, he mentioned “no” when I asked him to wash his hands. But then, with the promise of some lollipops, he reconsidered. Hands washed, he immediately ran to my 6-month-old in her bouncer. And yes, he went for her T-zone, but hey, at least his hands were clean. I’ll take the win!

Happy Father’s Day, from one cool dad to the next.

If you follow Fatherly’s Instagram handle, you may notice that we’ve been talking to a number of cool dads lately. We start by asking them about some of the little things that bring us the most joy, like the best movie to watch with your kid (among the answers, The Princess Bride, Zootopia, Sketch, Hook), the clothing they’re passionate about (black t-shirts, black button downs, and Jordan 1s are popular) and the music we blast for our kids (from Michal Jackson to Nirvana, Chance the Rapper to The Lone Bellow).

It has been revealed that but look past these small insights and you’ll find successful men who are eager to talk about their kids. The variety of responses show how every dad has their own take, their unique philosophy about being a good man, a strong partner, and a great parent. It also shows how much solidarity there is in being a dad.

Max Holloway, the dominant UFC fighter notes he believes in being strict, but “it’s not just me being hard on him and busting his chops, but also encouraging him and telling him he did a good job.”.

Tony Hale, who needs no introduction if you’re a fan of Toy Story, Arrested Development, or Veep, admits he was more of a helicopter parent, one whose kids—now in college—know that, "Hey, when you need me, I'm always going to be here.”.

Colton Underwood, the former reality star and pro football player is serious about the job: “I have the responsibility that he grows up to be a great human being that does good in the world.” While Maurice Edu, who you’ve no doubt been hearing calling the World Cup shots on Fox Sports, finds fatherhood to be fairly effortless because “I always knew I wanted to be a father, but until I actually became one, I didn't realize how much I wanted it.".

Minneapolis lawyer and former mayoral candidate Jazz Hampton believes that “Fatherhood is how you show up for your own kids and the rest of the world as well, and how you teach your kids to show up for other people.” Meanwhile, the “Tired Dad” Jon Gustin notes that parenting is tough, but rewarding — a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.”.

It has been revealed that then there’s Tom Llamas, our latest Cool Dad and the anchor of "NBC Nightly News” and "Top Story with Tom Llamas" on NBC News NOW. In a recent chat, Llamas reminded me that we, dads who are parenting now in 2026, weren’t the first and won’t be the last. Our parents struggled and cared and went through it all with their kids, and so did their dads, and theirs before them.

Industry observers note that llamas’ father, a Cuban refugee and dentist, was a major role model to him. “I learned a lot of great lessons from my dad,” Llamas says, “and then also try to be a better dad, and I think that's what my dad tried to do, too. He had a good dad, but he tried to be a better dad, and I'm trying to do the same thing.”.

Sources indicate that tom Llamas’ parents fled Cuba for Florida during Fidel Castro’s takeover of the country. Years later, in 1979, Tom was born. Llamas remembers a childhood in Miami that was a stark contrast to life in Cuba, under the rule of a dictator in a harsh economic economic environment. Primarily, he remembers his parents being there for him. “They would close the office early, like when I had sports, you know, to go and see me. Or if I had a school event they would close the office early, and for a small business that's income that you're not bringing in.”.

Recent findings suggest that tom Llamas and family. Credit: NBC.

He continues, “I'm grateful to have parents that always supported me in whatever I wanted to do — whether it was playing sports as a little boy, or when I got into journalism, or when I was into speech and debate in high school, to helping me when I had internships, because back when I was an intern you would not get paid.”.

Recent findings suggest that llamas says he now lives and breathes this family-first philosophy himself. The other night Llamas, who now lives in Latest York, anchored from the World Cup in Los Angeles and went to the game. “But then that same night, I jumped on a red eye so I could be home for a 9 AM little league game, and that's not something that that anyone has to ask me for — that's something I want to do, because I just believe that that kind of stuff needs to be automatic.”.

Industry observers note that this Father’s Day, Llamas has a message for all the dads out there: “It is the best job in the world to be a father [but] give yourself some grace cause it's really tough out there. There's a lot of books and opinions and podcasts and all kinds of things that are trying to tell people how to [parent] and I think, you know, just enjoy your time with your kids. Because it goes by very fast, and I truly think the greatest thing in the world is to be a dad.”.

Whether your baby will be born in December, or you just love the holidays that much.

Of course when parents are thinking about what to name their newly introduced baby, they look toward the things they value most. Whether it’s a lifelong love of literature, a sentimental meaning, or simply a certain vibe that fits your lifestyle, choosing a name you really adore often starts with thinking about what already brings you happiness. And for some parents, that means Christmas. It’s a holiday all about togetherness, giving, joy, tradition — all wonderful values on their own. For many, Christmastime is also a source of some of their best memories of a magical childhood. It’s easy to see why parents might choose a Christmas-adjacent baby name, and Noel is not the one and only option. Here are some of our favorites:.

This beautiful, classic girl’s name means “bright” or “clear.” And yes, Christmas is all about being merry and bright, but the real Christmas connection here is that Clara is the main character of the iconic Christmas ballet, The Nutcracker.

Douglas is a Scottish name meaning “dark stream.” But if you’re a Christmas lover, you’ll know that Douglas firs are an American evergreen tree species. This name is perfect if you love traditional boy names and would prefer one with a built-in nod to your favorite holiday.

Like the North Pole, of course! Kim Kardashian made the name popular when she gave it to her eldest child back in 2013, but now it feels like enough of a name that it wouldn’t be automatically associated with the young celeb.

If the Christmas story holds meaning for you, but naming your baby Mary or Joseph is a little too on the nose, consider Shepherd. It’s an occupation name (very trendy in recent years), and kind of doubles as a last name baby name too. But really, the shepherds in the fields were the first to hear the news of baby Jesus’s birth.

Do any of these names feel like the perfect pick for your little cherub?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article is sponsored by Eight Sleep. Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

Alexandra Zatarain helped build Eight Sleep into a tech unicorn, and she’s expecting her first child in January. Going through pregnancy while running a global organization has reshaped how she sees her own body, her industry and the product she’s building. On this episode of The Motherly Podcast, the co-founder of the sleep-technology company talks about the research that highlighted Eight Sleep’s technology was improving men’s sleep more than women’s and what the company did about it, why sleep is the most notable thing women can protect, and the career advice she wishes more women heard before becoming mothers.

Sources indicate that meet the expert: Alexandra Zatarain is the co-founder and VP of brand and marketing at Eight Sleep, the sleep-technology manufacturer behind the Pod. The Pod is an intelligent mattress cover that cools or heats each side to your ideal temperature automatically, maximizing deep sleep and minimizing wake-ups. A marketer and brand builder, she grew Eight Sleep from launch into a tech unicorn and helped create what the company calls the sleep fitness movement. Eight Sleep now sells in 37 countries. She’s expecting her first child in January with her husband, Matteo, the company’s co-founder and CEO.

Alexandra Zatarain: So many things. I just turned 37, and I’ve seen so many friends go through pregnancy before me. After my first trimester, I felt so bad, thinking, what a terrible friend I was. When you haven’t experienced it, you have such little empathy for what a woman’s body is going through, especially when life keeps demanding so much of you and it doesn’t stop. I really didn’t understand that you could feel so different in your body for so long. It’s built so much more admiration for women and what we go through, and it’s let me embrace a feminine side of myself that in tech you usually don’t get to bring out.

Alexandra Zatarain: It’s made me realize that the only way the world out there is going to change for our benefit as women and mothers is if more of us are the ones making the decisions. I just don’t see any way around it. We have a lot of parents at Eight Sleep, every executive on our team is a parent, but as a woman the experience is completely different. Unless we can share that first-hand knowledge, it’s going to be hard to make progress as fast as we need to. It’s unfortunate that it takes the first-person experience to become that advocate, because everyone should appreciate what mothers go through, given that we all come from a mother.

In a recent development, alexandra Zatarain: A couple of years ago, our clinical team, which is more than 90% women, was analyzing data from our user base and noticed our technology had been improving men’s sleep more than women’s. They asked, what are we missing in how we design this? It turned out the algorithms that manage temperature while you sleep had been fed more data representing men than women. That’s a classic problem in science, where women are underrepresented because our bodies are more complex. You have to account for where someone is in their hormonal journey, pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopause. So we invested a couple million dollars into research and developed features from it. That changed how we think about ourselves, less about helping everyone in a broad way and more about solving specific problems women have had for ages.

Alexandra Zatarain: Sleep is the most key pillar of health. You would die sooner from sleep deprivation than from food deprivation, which tells you how fundamental it is. For women it matters even more because our hormones rule our lives, and sleep is the one tool we have to regulate them. If you sleep well, your chances of better hormonal balance go up significantly. It’s the best medicine we have, more than working out, more than any meal. The challenge is that those same hormones are often playing against us, making it harder to sleep well in different seasons of life, so keeping our routines as stable as possible helps counter what our bodies are going through.

Alexandra Zatarain: The mindset piece is really important. There’s so much going on, the anxiety, the intrusive thoughts, so not being too hard on yourself is the first step. Understanding that the season will pass should put you a little more at ease, because it’s not going to be your life forever. The other piece is setting yourself up with the right systems, and the most important one is available to everyone for free, which is routine. It helps your body a lot. When you do need to sleep, it’ll be easier for your body to fall asleep because it’s used to the schedule.

Recent findings suggest that alexandra Zatarain: I’m very rigid about my sleep schedule. I travel a lot, so sleep is number one for me. I make space for eight to nine hours every night, and I’m pretty good at hitting it. I go to bed by 9:30 or 10 every single night no matter where I am in the world, and I don’t really use an alarm unless I have to wake up before 6, because my body just wakes up on its own. That schedule is the thing that’s changed my life the most. Second to that is the environment, the temperature in my room and my bed, the lights going dark, no noise.

Alexandra Zatarain: I think of myself as an athlete, and we’re all sort of athletes in a way. My sport is making decisions about how to build this business, and that means I have to train, stay healthy and think long term. It’s not a sprint. We’ve been doing this for 12 years, so the question is how do I not burn out and stay here 20 or 30 years more. I’m also lucky I built this with my husband, so there’s no real line between business and personal life for us. It’s all mixed in, but it’s so purpose-driven that achieving that purpose every day is what feeds the energy.

Alexandra Zatarain: I’m very open with them about how intentional I was. I did my embryo freezing in my early 30s because of where I was in life. And I tell them that if they want a career after they have a family, the best time to build equity in that career is to push as hard as you can before. Know what you want, because time isn’t always on our side as women. Move up the ranks, so that by the time you have kids you have more flexibility and maybe a higher income. It is possible, but it takes planning, it will require compromises, and very importantly it will require the right partner.

Industry observers note that alexandra Zatarain: It starts with the people around you understanding what you truly need. Sometimes it’s as simple as the encouragement of, yes, go take a nap, yes, your body’s going through a lot. It gets harder once the baby’s home and the mom is maybe exclusively breastfeeding, because it really all falls on you. So have a blueprint in place ahead of time for how the load is going to be shared. Our partners are much more involved than previous generations, so have those conversations early. It doesn’t end with the birth plan. That’s where everything starts.

It put me in the trajectory to build the team that would make it possible for me to become a mother, to figure out what to delegate and who to elevate, and I’ve built a stronger team as a result. But the biggest thing is that it’s taught me to let go. I can’t control how I feel every day. As a Type A person I always want to be in control, and this has been like therapy, learning that I’m not in control of my body. I’m building a human, and it’s fine if for this season things just work differently.

From activewear to snacks to the crucial stuff we all forget about, here’s your complete product guide to the gear your young athlete needs.

Sources indicate that A good water bottle is the first thing every young athlete needs, and the first thing they will leave on a bench somewhere. Look for one that is durable, easy to clean, and massive enough to get them through practice.

Recent findings suggest that the 50-ounce size gives kids enough water for long practices and tournament days, and the tethered leakproof cap means one less loose lid rolling around the car. It is also lightweight, clippable, and dishwasher-safe, which matters because no parent needs another thing that requires special handling.

Recent findings suggest that some practices are long, hot, and sweaty enough that water alone may not cut it. A sports drink can help replace electrolytes when sweat is doing most of the work.

Recent findings suggest that this variety pack has electrolytes, with no added sugar and no artificial sweeteners, flavors, or dyes. At 20 calories per bottle, it is a lighter sports-drink option for parents who want hydration help without sending a kid into practice with something that looks like melted candy.

In a recent development, some sports days run straight through the normal eating schedule, which is how kids end up starving in the car and furious at everyone. In a recent development, this sunscreen is fast-absorbing, nongreasy, and water- and sweat-resistant for up to 80 minutes, which makes it a practical fit for practices and games. Supergoop is made for face and body, so kids do not need separate bottles.

It has been revealed that A school backpack is already doing too much. A dedicated sports bag gives clothes, towels, water bottles, deodorant, and gear somewhere to live that is not the floor of your car.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.
  • Recent findings suggest that my 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me.
  • According to recent reports, to which I say: We manage just fine, thanks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.

Recent findings suggest that my 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me. I like cuddling him all night, and I’ve come to accept that it’s just the kind of mom I am: the clingy co-sleeping type. When he was littler, we took safe-sleep precautions with a bassinet and all that jazz, but these days, he sleeps right up next to me. Most non-co-sleeping families cringe at this. And then they immediately want to know: So how do you get intimate with your partner?

According to recent reports, to which I say: We manage just fine, thanks. But lately, I’ve been wondering about the elephant in the room. Or, should I say, the toddler.

According to recent reports, my husband and I NEVER have sex in the bed with our toddler. But we do sneak into the bathroom. Or sometimes, once he’s deeply asleep, we pull out a cot on the other side of the room and get it on in the dark. I’m embarrassed even admitting that.

I also don’t believe we’re the only parents who have ever found themselves in this predicament.

Here’s the thing... our house isn’t huge. And between the 3-year-old sleeping soundly in our blacked-out bedroom and one of our much more aware older kids wandering out of their rooms, we’ve chosen the former.

Sources indicate that which brings me to something else we really need to address. What about the “olden days”? Ma and Pa from Little House on the Prairie managed to have four babies while living in one-room log cabins and shanties. I guarantee they weren’t heading out to the barn or the outhouse every time they wanted to have sex, especially when bears and wolves were roaming around, and temperatures dipped below zero.

Besides, many modern families around the world still live and sleep in shared spaces.

It has been revealed that lately I’ve wondered if being horrified by the idea of parents having sex in the same room as a sleeping child is a cultural thing. Is it so awful if they’re still very little? At what point does “they have no idea what’s happening” turn into “Mom and Dad need to find somewhere else to do this”?

We reached out to experts to answer all the questions you’ve probably been dying to know but have been way too embarrassed to ask.

It has been revealed that here’s the short answer: Parents don’t need to feel guilty about having sex in the same room as a newborn or young infant. An infant doesn’t have the “cognitive capacity to understand what sex is,” and they won’t remember or understand what’s going on, indicates Kimberly Resnick Anderson, LCSW, an AASECT-certified sex therapist.

In a recent development, anderson does add one caveat, though. Having a baby nearby is likely to make parents more reserved and overall less expressive during sex. Over time, she claims, that could potentially lead to a “more permanent shift” in how they express themselves sexually.

When does she recommend finding some privacy? Around age 1.

Once a child develops language and becomes mobile, she claims, it becomes harder to get it on, knowing the child could wake up in the middle of it.

But Samantha Ridout, M.Phil., BCBA, a child development and behavioral expert, cautions against treating any birthday as a universal cutoff. No two children develop at exactly the same rate, she notes, so there isn’t a magical age when a child suddenly becomes aware of what’s happening around them. Instead, parents should watch for their child’s growing alertness and awareness and set appropriate boundaries.

It has been revealed that I’ve found this to be true in my own family. We moved our older two kids out of our room quicker because they were definitely more aware than our last, who just feels more “babyish.”.

But both experts made one thing very clear: During sex, infants need to be in a separate, safe sleep space.

Let’s go back to my Ma and Pa observation for a minute, shall we?

The idea of children and adults having separate bedrooms is a relatively latest phenomenon, claims Macall Gordon, a researcher and sleep coach with an undergraduate degree in anthropology who studies children’s sleep through a sociohistorical lens. She says before the lightbulb was invented, family life revolved around sunrise and sunset, with families often sleeping in shared spaces.

Industry observers note that but with electricity, adults could suddenly stay up after children went to bed, she adds. Now, children needed a “separate space to sleep” while adults stayed up. So the nursery and the crib came along. Then, she claims, the layout of homes started to change, too, to include hallways connecting separate rooms. Before that, rooms were all connected to each other, so you had to go through one to get to another.

To this day, however, a separate bedroom is still something of a privilege. Many families simply don’t have “extra, separate rooms,” Gordon points out, especially in massive cities, where studios and lofts are common, or in cultures where extended family members may occupy additional bedrooms. “While we think of a separate room for children as the norm, it really wasn’t for most of our history,” Gordon shares.

According to recent reports, tiffany Belanger, cosleeping expert and founder of Cosleepy, notes the topic tends to divide her followers into two camps: those who will have sex in the room with a kid and those who won’t. When I described my scenario to her, she responded that floor sex while young kids are still sleeping in their parents’ bed is actually pretty common among the co-sleeping families she hears from.

You want to know if mine has woken up before.

But rarely. He’s a really deep sleeper, and it’s only happened a few times. It’s dark, and when he did wake up, he immediately called out for me in that disoriented, half-asleep way toddlers do. We stopped immediately. The cot is also on the far side of the bed, outside his line of sight. As far as I know, he never saw or heard anything.

Recent findings suggest that will we emotionally damage our kid if he were to catch us in the act? Unlikely, Ridout indicates, if parents stay calm, stop immediately, tell the child they are safe, and answer their questions in a simple, non-panicky way.

But all of this still leaves me with the extremely practical question that got us into this mess in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that parents have to get creative, flexible, and spontaneous, claims Anderson. That might mean asking family or friends to babysit when you can, doing it in other rooms, or using whatever short pockets of privacy you can find.

Industry observers note that and while Belanger reassures me that my floor-sex solution isn't unheard of among co-sleeping parents, the other experts think it’s not a great option when kids become mobile and verbal. So, I suppose it might be time to retire the cot. Where to next?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand.
  • Here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing... or 10.

Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand. Sure, I loved the cheeky ads where an American football coach goes to England to manage a football club. But the premise felt too thin to flesh out into a full series, and Jason Sudeikis’ body of work up to that point didn’t inspire confidence that a sitcom based on the character could hold my attention.

I couldn’t have been more wrong.

Here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood. Not in a neat, Hallmark-movie kind of way, but in the messy, long-distance, guilt-soaked, love-you-so-much-it-hurts way that a lot of us actually live it. Ted’s relationship with his son, Henry — conducted mostly through grainy FaceTime calls across a six-hour time difference — is the quiet beating heart of all three seasons.

While the rest of AFC Richmond is arguing about formations and tabloid covers, Ted is trying to figure out how to be a good dad from 4,000 miles away while working through how his relationship with his own father has formed him.

Sources indicate that the man is not perfect. Nobody raising kids is, and running off to London without your family to accept a job you’re wholly unqualified for as an act of emotional avoidance is a narrative necessity, but it’s a flaw many folks have pointed out.

But along the way, he does his best and makes the right plays in the moments that count. And since parenting lessons wrapped inside a feel-good soccer comedy are my personal favorite delivery mechanism, let’s run through 10 times Ted Lasso gave us a genuine master class in this whole dad thing.

Industry observers note that it’s Ted’s first night in London. He’s jet-lagged and disoriented, and the very first thing he does is call home to Henry. He fumbles the time zones and sounds a little lost, but he makes sure his kid hears his voice before the day is out.

There’s a version of Ted Lasso in a different corner of the multiverse who gets swept up in the fresh job, the new city, the chaos of it all, and phones it in on the fatherhood front. This Ted doesn’t. He knows that presence isn’t always physical. Sometimes it’s a crackling FaceTime connection at midnight your time, 6 a.m. their time, just so your kid knows you’re still there.

According to recent reports, henry, during a video call, asks his dad if he’s ever run into The Beatles over there in England and whether he can get a photo with John, Paul, George, and Ringo. Now, Ted knows that both John Lennon and George Harrison have been dead for decades. He also knows his kid is 8 years old and asking with complete, genuine wonder. So Ted just agrees to try. He doesn't have the heart to kill that particular joy right now.

This one is subtle, but it matters. There's a real parenting skill in knowing when the truth can wait five minutes and when it needs to be delivered immediately. Ted isn't being dishonest — he's being developmentally attuned. There's a season for everything, as a certain king once sang from the stage of a Broadway house, and this particular season called for letting a little kid's imagination breathe. Ted will level with Henry about the hard stuff — and he does, plenty of times — but he picks his moments. That's wisdom.

When Michelle and Henry show up in London, Ted drops everything. They swing by the Crown and Anchor for an authentic English pub experience. They build a double-decker bus model at the kitchen table. And Henry settles into his happy place, sleeping between his parents. Even though Ted is in the midst of a brutal season, managing a locker room full of fragile egos while racking up losses, none of that matters for those few days. He is simply Dad.

In a recent development, what makes this moment rich is what we know that Henry doesn't: His parents' marriage is already over. Michelle is about to tell Ted she wants a divorce. And yet Ted keeps the joy intact for his son. He doesn't let his own grief occupy the visit. That is an act of real parenting discipline — the ability to compartmentalize your own pain long enough to give your child a memory that isn't shadowed by yours. Most of us have had to do some version of this. It doesn't feel heroic in the moment. It just feels hard. Ted does it anyway.

Henry asks Ted why, whenever he sees him on TV coaching soccer, he never seems to be doing anything. It's a kid's question, but it's actually a perfect question. Ted's answer is one of the most quietly profound things in the entire series. He tells Henry that once the game starts, he can't really tell his players what to do — he just has to hope that everything he's been trying to teach them made some kind of dent. Then he claims: “It's kind of like being a father.”.

And then Henry, having absorbed none of this, is clearly already thinking about something else entirely. Ted realizes midsentence that his kid has mentally bounced. He stops talking. He smiles. He gets it. That moment is the whole job description of parenthood distilled into 30 seconds of television. You pour yourself into the role and hope it lands. You accept that you can't control the outcome. And you find a way to laugh about it — or at least smile — when your kid demonstrates, in real time, that they were not listening. Every parent reading this has lived this exact moment.

Henry isn’t the first kid to idolize a less-than-stellar role model, but his admiration for Jamie Tartt is a particular form of torture for Ted. As enigmatic as he is talented, Jamie makes Ted’s life incredibly difficult, even when he’s scoring goals. This puts Ted in a tough spot as Henry enthusiastically belts out the terribly annoying Baby Shark-themed Jamie Tartt song and sports his jersey with pride.

But Ted lets his son revel in the moment of having access to the talented and popular starlet. He doesn’t even hint at the fact that perhaps Tartt isn’t the best guy to look up to. And when Jamie flashes Ted a smirk that makes his beautiful face even more punchable than usual while signing Henry’s jersey, Ted takes a deep breath and lets his son have a moment he’ll never forget.

Recent findings suggest that ted gets word from Michelle that Henry has been involved in a bullying situation at school — and then discovers it wasn't Henry who was bullied. Henry was the bully. Ted is shaken. And because of schedules and time zones, he has difficulty getting in touch with Henry right away.

Industry observers note that if Ted had been around, he would likely have responded emotionally and sucked all the air out of the room. But when father and son finally get a chance to talk, Henry admits he messed up and didn't follow his dad's advice to count to 10 when he gets angry.

According to recent reports, with a little bit of forced space, Henry comes back around on his own. Ted doesn't strip his son of dignity while correcting him. And when Henry apologizes to his friend Doug with a rap in front of the class, you can almost hear Ted beaming through the phone. The lesson Ted had been repeating wasn't wasted — it just needed more time to work. Be a goldfish, sure, but also trust that the seeds you plant eventually grow. Even in the hardest soil.

According to recent reports, when Michelle and Henry leave London at the end of their visit, Ted walks them to the gate, knowing his marriage is essentially over and that his son doesn't know it. He notes goodbye to Henry the way you say goodbye when you're not sure when you'll see each other again — fully present, holding it together, promising to talk soon. He watches Henry walk away with the airport attendant. And then the mask slips, just for a moment, and you see how much it costs him.

Sources indicate that here's what Ted doesn't do: He doesn't make the goodbye about himself. He doesn't get weepy in a way that burdens Henry with having to manage his father's emotions. He saves that for after the kid is out of sight. This is something parents don't talk about enough — the emotional labor of keeping your own grief off your child's plate. It's not suppression. It's protection. There's a version of this that's emotionally avoidant and unhealthy, but Ted's version in this moment is clear-eyed and loving. He feels everything. He just knows whose feelings need managing right now.

According to recent reports, after Henry's visit to London ends and the lad heads back to Kansas, Ted does something small and wonderful. He indicates Henry, via video call, that he's placed the miniature Premier League Lego trophy Henry gave him into the Nelson Road Stadium Lego set they built together. It's a tiny thing. It's also everything.

Recent findings suggest that physical objects carry emotional weight for kids in ways that words sometimes can't. That Lego stadium becomes a shared artifact. It’s something Henry can picture when he thinks of his dad. Something that notes “you were here, and you matter, and I kept a piece of what we made.”.

It's the parenting equivalent of keeping a drawing on the fridge forever. Henry even notices that Nate's Lego figure is at the back of the bench and asks about it, which gives Ted a gentle opening to explain that relationships can change without anyone being erased. Heavy stuff, delivered through the medium of tiny plastic soccer coaches.

According to recent reports, during their Lego video call conversation, Ted tells Henry that he doesn't love the idea of being away from him and that the only reason he's staying in England is that he's doing something important. Henry — who is, let's remember, about 10 years old — tells his dad to try to win the whole thing. Ted pushes back, saying winning isn't everything. And Henry says, essentially: “OK, but at least try.”.

It has been revealed that that's the moment a kid flips the script on you, and you realize they've been absorbing your lessons all along and also developing their own perspective on top of them. Ted doesn't dismiss the advice. He doesn't say “thanks, buddy” in that patronizing way parents sometimes do. He actually sits with it. He lets Henry be right.

Kids need to see their parents receive feedback and adjust — it's how they learn that it's a normal and healthy thing to do. Plus, Henry is objectively correct. You can care about more than winning and still bring your whole effort to the field. That's not a contradiction. That's maturity.

Ted walks away from AFC Richmond. He turns down the job. He gets on the plane. He comes home to Kansas and, within about 60 seconds, is coaching Henry's junior league team, running plays, completely in his element.

In a recent development, but the real parenting lesson isn't just that Ted comes home. It's why he comes home. He doesn't do it because the job went badly or because England rejected him. He does it because he looked at his life clearly and made an honest accounting of what mattered most. He indicated his son — showed Henry in the most concrete way possible — that he is the priority. Not in the abstract, inspirational-poster way. In the literal, I-quit-my-dream-job-in-London-to-be-at-your-soccer-games way.

And then in the finale's final image, when Henry misses a shot and gets frustrated, Ted calls him over. Henry says the words Ted has been saying all series — be a goldfish — and they both smile.

The lesson came back home. Same as the dad.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more. Experts share how to shop less and still feed your family well.

Industry observers note that it’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks. Worse, you then have to play budget Tetris, moving money around to make sure you have funds for the inevitable grocery run you’ll have to make next week. Add in the gas it takes to get to and from, and you’re spent literally and figuratively.

The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever. And, sure, cutting back on trips is probably one of the easiest and most logical ways to save money (and time, and sanity). But it begs the question: How long can you go between grocery runs without your family surviving on cereal benders?

We asked food and budgeting experts how they personally make it work.

Most of the experts we polled said one significant shop a week is sort of the sweet spot. “Every extra trip not only takes up valuable time, but is also another chance to grab things that aren’t on the list and drive up your overall grocery bill,” says Laurie Hise, CEO of Passionate Penny Pincher.

It has been revealed that is it possible to stretch it to every two weeks? Maybe. But AJ Prasaguet, head of the iconic Palace bar and restaurant in Miami Beach, points out that biweekly shopping “can work if you have the storage space, freezer capacity, and money available upfront. Those are real considerations, and not every household has all three.”.

Recent findings suggest that amber Hanson, a licensed nutritionist and founder of Whole You Nutrition, emphasizes that there’s no cut-and-dry, one-size-fits-all answer. Your ideal grocery-shopping cadence will ultimately depend on things like how close you live to a store and when your paycheck hits the bank. If you get paid every two weeks, it might make sense to shop on that timeframe too.

Before you make your little grocery list and head to the store, open up your own fridge, freezer, and pantry. “The best way to save money is to use what you have already paid for,” indicates Hanson.

Sources indicate that jenn Lueke, Fresh York Times-bestselling author of Don’t Think About Dinner, does her inventory every Friday night, then builds the next week’s meals around what’s left. Example: “If I know I have a half carton of broth that needs to be used, I’ll make sure to pick up a grain, like rice or quinoa, that I can cook in it.”.

According to recent reports, prasaguet goes one step further. “Give an ingredient its next job before you buy it. If a recipe needs half a container of something, decide where the other half is going.” Take cabbage, for instance. It can be slaw one night, stir-fry the next, and soup filler after that.

Another tip Hise is a fan of is ordering online for pickup or delivery when you can. The simple act of skipping the aisles means you don't have to worry about impulse buys wreaking havoc on your total.

According to recent reports, as a busy working mom who regularly feels she has to have everything for the week figured out at all times, this was very liberating to hear! As the experts remind us, life happens. Prepares change. A rigid seven-night menu is a fast track to wasted food.

Recent findings suggest that but if it makes you feel better to have the week mostly lined up, you could follow Hise’s example: plan five “fresh” dinners a week, leaving one night for leftovers and one for a meal pulled from what’s already in the pantry, fridge, or freezer. Prasaguet relies on a similar formula: four planned dinners, one leftovers meal, one pantry or freezer dinner, on flex night. “That gives the week some structure without pretending everything will go according to plan,” he indicates.

Lueke recommends starting with dinners, then exploring how you can make the most of them. “Will the slow-cooker chicken stretch to cover lunches for half the week too? Can I make a double batch of quinoa and bulk up our mid-week sheet pan dinner?” Theme nights like Taco Tuesday or Breakfast for Dinner also help reduce decision fatigue.

According to recent reports, the trick to making groceries last, many of the pros explained, is buying foods with different lifespans and eating them in the right order. “You do not want an entire cart of produce that all needs attention at once,” emphasizes Prasaguet.

Lueke thinks about it in three zones:.

Recent findings suggest that andrea Woroch, a consumer savings expert, notes that some hardy produce (think garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes, winter squash, even whole apples) can last for months depending on storage conditions as well as how they’re handled. For fast-spoilers like berries, resist the urge to buy the giant fresh packs unless you know your family will gobble them down. Otherwise, stock up on frozen.

If you're afraid frozen and canned food won't pack the same nutritional punch as fresh, well, the experts beg to differ.

“One of the biggest misconceptions about healthy eating is that fresh foods are always better than frozen or canned alternatives. That’s simply not the case,” indicates Jennifer Pallian, a registered dietitian and founder of Foodess. Frozen vegetables are typically flash-frozen shortly after harvest, and research has found they can be just as nutritious as fresh produce that’s been sitting in your fridge for several days. In some cases, they even have more vitamin C.”.

Don’t turn your nose up at canned staples, either. Pallian is a big proponent of canned light tuna (a solid source of protein, selenium, and omega-3s) and canned chickpeas, which pack both protein and fiber and are already cooked.

Just opt for low-sodium or no-salt-added canned veggies and beans, and be mindful of foods packed in juices, syrups, or sauces.

Adopting a few little habits can go a long way toward making food last until your next grocery run:.

However, Prasaguet reminds us, “Stretching groceries should never mean stretching food safety.” That means refrigerating leftovers within two hours, eating them within three to four days, or sticking them in the freezer.

According to recent reports, you should know that eating well doesn’t mean you have to buy a bunch of fancy superfoods. “Some of the most nutrient-dense foods in the grocery store are also the cheapest,” Hanson says.

Here’s what our experts say they keep stocked:.

It has been revealed that and while many of us think shopping in bulk must save money, Prasaguet notes that it’s “only better value if you can afford it, store it, and finish it.” Hise’s workaround is to grab a few extra cans whenever they’re on sale. “A few extra cans a month can add up to a pantry that carries you through a tight month.”.

If you feel like a failure every time you serve your family dinner out of a bag or can, it’s high time you cut yourself some slack.

Recent findings suggest that “Frozen and canned foods that you actually eat beat fresh vegetables you throw away every time,” states Hise. Link agrees, adding, “I’d much rather see a family use convenient foods they enjoy than buy fresh ingredients that become a science experiment in the crisper drawer.”.

“A fed family is a win, and ‘fresh’ isn’t the measure of a good dinner," Lueke puts it simply. A balanced meal is made up of a protein, a plant or two, and something filling. It truly does not matter if those came from the produce section or the freezer aisle.

According to recent reports, but maybe Prasaguet sums it up best. “You do not have to prove your love through a complicated dinner,” he reassures. “Feeding your family with the resources you have is already an act of care.”.

In a recent development, when you watch the hit Star Wars TV show The Mandalorian — or the fresh film The Mandalorian and Grogu — and you start to wonder if there’s something about being a bounty hunter with a heart of gold that can help you with youth sports, you’re not nuts. Industry observers note that as the summer starts to give way to the beginning of school, we reached out to Wayne to get his core principles as a longtime coach of youth sports. This man may know how to calm down Baby Yoda, but that’s just acting. As a soccer coach, Wayne is an even bigger expert. How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic

💡 Key Takeaways
