Forty-eight dogs â mostly French Bulldogs and English Bulldogs â found in what authorities are describing as a clandestine breeding operation in San Juan de Miraflores, Peru.

And when you read what was found, it is hard not to feel angry.

Authorities discovered the animals in appalling conditions on September 28 in an apartment on JirÃ³n Santiago RodrÃ­guez. The group included 25 French Bulldogs, nine English Bulldogs, eight mixed-breed dogs, five French Bulldog puppies, and one Dachshund. There was also a rooster. Local French Bulldog club, Club Frenchie, heard about the rescue through social media and immediately reached out to offer assistance. One member of the club spoke to a reporter from the Peruvian newspaper El Comercio about what they had witnessed:.

Industry observers note that âThe state of health was absolutely deplorable. There were dogs covered in feces, filthy, with no hygiene whatsoever, dogs with broken nails, bitten ears, and other serious problems,â he stated.

According to recent reports, the dogs were brought to the Municipal Veterinary Clinic in San Juan de Miraflores, where they were examined and received treatment for a range of conditions. Most were suffering from heat stress, and many had excessively long nails, some bleeding, skin problems, fungal issues, eye infections, surgical scars, and other conditions requiring medical attention. Six puppies reportedly needed incubator care, with two described as being in a particularly fragile condition.

It has been revealed that following the intervention, the animals were taken to the municipal veterinary service, and some have since been moved into foster care. The San Juan de Miraflores Provincial Corporate Criminal Prosecutor's Office is investigating the case, and FÃ©lix Sonco and Darlys Vanegas were arrested at the scene.

As if the horrendous conditions that greeted rescuers werenât disturbing enough, it appears that this wasnât simply a breeding operation, but an illegal, makeshift veterinary clinic.

Some of these dogs had undergone surgery on their vocal cords; a barbaric procedure known as debarking. Being kept in cramped and filthy conditions meant that these dogs were barking and crying constantly. Debarking was a way to reduce noise and avoid complaints.

They didnât improve conditions. They didnât provide relief. They simply removed their ability to voice their distress.

Sources indicate that evidence also suggests that several female Bulldogs were bred repeatedly, with some reportedly forced to carry as many as ten litters of puppies. Veterinary examination also found evidence that crude cesarean surgeries had been performed prematurely to get puppies out faster and back on the market, while the mothers, if they survived, were bred again.

Investigators reportedly found premature newborn puppies inside an unsterilized incubator, while puppies were being sold for around 1,500 to 2,500 Peruvian soles each â roughly $400 to $670 USD.

French Bulldogs and English Bulldogs are brachycephalic breeds. Their shortened skull and squishy faces are a significant part of their appeal. But there is a very uncomfortable truth behind that cute face.

That same anatomy that many people find irresistible can make it harder for a dog to breathe, exercise, sleep, regulate their body temperature, and, in some cases, give birth.

We have to stop pretending these things are simply âpart of being a Bulldog.â.

A dog struggling to breathe is not just a snorer. A dog that overheats easily is not just âsensitive to the heat.â These are medical problems.

Brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS) refers to the conditions that affect breeds with a shortened skull, or âbrachycephaly.â These conditions include hypoplastic trachea (narrow  windpipe), stenotic nares (narrow nostrils), and a tongue and soft palate that are too large and long for the mouth, resulting in obstruction of the airways and difficulty swallowing.

It has been revealed that these complications have led many veterinary professionals and animal welfare advocates to question the ethics of breeding these dogs. When a physical characteristic can affect basic functions like breathing and temperature regulation, choosing which dogs reproduce needs to consider more than appearance.

That little flat face. Those big eyes. The stout little body. The funny little snorts.

According to recent reports, most people see cute, even adorable. But as veterinarians, we see a whole list of problems that need to be monitored.

A Bulldog can be an absolutely wonderful companion and still have anatomy that puts them at risk for serious health problems. Breeding of these dogs should require more responsibility, not less, with breeders selecting for less extreme conformations.

According to recent reports, there is something very sad about how much importance we place on how dogs look. A certain face. A certain size. A certain coat. A certain breed.

Recent findings suggest that the more desirable that look becomes, the more money there is in producing it. That creates a market, and unfortunately, where there is money, there will always be those willing to cut corners.

According to recent reports, this does not mean that every breeder is bad. There are responsible breeders who health-test their dogs, carefully select breeding pairs, provide appropriate veterinary care, and take responsibility for the puppies they bring into the world. Those who are actively trying to breed healthier versions of dogs whose health and function have been crippled through selective breeding for exaggerated features.

Puppy mills are something very different.

The problem is when the animals producing those puppies become a means to an end.

A female dog becomes a breeding machine.

And veterinary care becomes an expense to minimize or avoid, not an essential part of responsible animal care.

When it comes to looking for your next four-legged family member, start your search at an animal shelter. Research your favorite breed and know how to recognize a suspicious situation.

If you are planning to purchase or adopt a puppy, you should be able to inspect the home or facility where the puppy was raised, and meet the puppyâs mother. Breeders who are unwilling or unable to allow this raise suspicions of unethical practice, and if you are concerned about a potential welfare matter, donât be tempted to buy a puppy to ârescueâ it â this simply finances the operation. Instead, contact your local animal control agency, humane society, sheriff, or police department.

When extreme conformation interferes with breathing and thermoregulation, when it increases the risk of difficult births and chronic airway problems, we need to consider whether breeding these dogs is the right thing to do. But if people will buy them, people will breed them.

Itâs up to us to look past the adorable face we saw on Instagram and ask:.

Are they breathing comfortably?

Do they have functional airways?

And, as the horrific plight of these 48 dogs reminds us, where did they come from?

Loving Bulldogs is not the problem.

The problem is loving an appearance so much that we stop asking what that appearance means for the animal.

These dogs have been through a terrible situation, but now they have a chance.

In a recent development, they need veterinary care. Their nails need treatment, their skin and eyes need evaluation, their nutritional needs need to be addressed, and their other medical problems need to be properly investigated. Some require specialized treatment, while others are recovering in foster homes.

And hopefully, many of these dogs will eventually experience something that should have been completely ordinary from the beginning:.

It has been revealed that these dogs were not born to produce puppies. They were not born to be quiet. They were not born to look a certain way for someone else's profit.

For that reason, adoption should always be considered before buying a puppy.

According to recent reports, there are so many wonderful dogs already waiting in shelters, foster homes, and recovering from neglect. Dogs that may not have the perfect face or pedigree but have an enormous capacity to love.

They don't need to be produced.

Please, before asking where to buy the puppy with the cutest face, ask who is already waiting for someone to choose them.

8 Easy Landscape Designer Tricks to Transition Your Garden From Fall into Winter

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While you might be thinking that the gardening season is drawing to a close this month, there's plenty to look forward to, especially if make a few simple switches to help your yard transition from fall into winter.
  • It has been revealed that check through our landscape designer tricks to take a fall yard into winter, and add one or two to your outside space now.
  • Consider, too, how to make your fall garden user-friendly so you feel inspired to spend plenty of time outside still, perhaps by including a cosy gathering area around a fire pit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While you might be thinking that the gardening season is drawing to a close this month, there's plenty to look forward to, especially if make a few simple switches to help your yard transition from fall into winter. As the year segues into the cooler months, it's time to enjoy colorful stems, textural bark, sculptural seedheads and shrubs bejewelled with bright berries, and relish the quiet beauty of this season.

It has been revealed that check through our landscape designer tricks to take a fall yard into winter, and add one or two to your outside space now. An injection of structural evergreens, naturalistic ornamental grasses, a tree with fiery foliage or colorful autumn bulbs can make a huge difference at this time of year now the late-season flower show is coming to an end.

Consider, too, how to make your fall garden user-friendly so you feel inspired to spend plenty of time outside still, perhaps by including a cosy gathering area around a fire pit. Which of these easy tricks landscape designers use to carry a garden from fall into winter are right for your yard?

Recent findings suggest that adding a mix of ornamental grasses is a fundamental element of fall garden design and these low-maintenance plants will continue to look good all through winter. While many annual and perennial flowering plants will happily grow through airy grasses in summer, the blades will keep borders looking full once they've finish blooming.

Choose varieties that offer bold autumn color such as Panicum virgatum ‘Shenandoah’, available from Nature Hills. Also known as switch grass, this well-behaved clump-forming grass develops stunning red and damson tones in fall, topped by wiry stems of flowers. Reaching 3 feet high, it looks fabulous planted among taller shrubs as well as with perennial blooms.

Another option favored by landscape designers is blue-green-leaved Festuca glauca 'Elijah Blue', also available from Nature Hills. Growing to just a foot high, it's perfect for border edges and winter containers.

It has been revealed that landscape designers often choose trees with fiery foliage to create a stunning focal point with brilliant shades of scarlet, russet, gold or burgundy. Even if space is limited, there are plenty of smaller trees that will squeeze into a compact garden.

It has been revealed that some of most spectacular fall color is typically associated with Acer (maple) trees, but to carry the interest on into winter, choose a type with textural bark, too. Acer griseum, the paperbark maple and available from Plant Addicts, has peeling, papery warm-brown bark. Caught in the light of a low winter sun, its peeling curls of bark are nothing short of spectacular. The coral bark Japanese maple, available from trees.com, has bark in an intense red tone that's equally eye-catching.

Another option if you're wondering what to plant in fall is a multi-trunked tree that, once the bright foliage has fallen, brings architectural interest to your garden, like the Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry tree, available from trees.com.

According to recent reports, attractively planted container gardens are a landscape designer's best friend during the cooler months of the year. These portable pots of color and texture can be positioned wherever you want, adding a welcoming touch to an entrance or a bright splash to a patio table.

In a recent development, there are all sorts of vibrant plants that love life in a patio pot and last from fall into winter for a wonderful cool-season display. The go-to formula is to combine a thriller (height), filler (body) and spiller (edging) to create a full, textured look. Good choices for fall and winter include compact evergreens or ornamental grasses to add the height element, pansies to fill out the body of the planter, and ivy to tumble over the edges. For a modern look, squeezing a container full of a single variety is an even easier option.

Industry observers note that dwarf pine trees are enjoying a surge in popularity with landscape designers, and no wonder. While in spring, summer and fall they provide a green, textural foil to colorful flowers and leaves, once winter arrives they emerge as standout sculptural shapes. The beauty of slow-growing dwarf pines is that they naturally stay compact and well-shaped, so need very little looking after.

Dwarf Mugo pine (Pinus mugo var. pumilo) is a particular favorite thanks to its dense, dark needles. While it eventually grows to 3-5 feet high, its easily kept pruned into a neat mound. Dwarf Mugo pine, available from trees.com, keeps its seed cones all through winter, adding to the display. Adding one, or an odd number dotted through your outside space, is a great way to ensure your garden has character throughout the year, and helps avoid that sensation of sparseness that often happens in winter when many plants are dormant.

Recent findings suggest that when summer perennials and annuals fade you will need something else to take their place. Autumn-flowering bulbs will pop up reliably year after year to add color and, if you choose the right sunny spot, will naturalise, gently spreading to reflect how comfortable they are in your landscape. This repetition will strengthen the planting design, as well as adding continuity.

It has been revealed that nerine bowdenii (also known as as Bowden lily) brings an explosion of color to rejuvenate tired fall borders. These beautiful bright blooms on sturdy stems grow to 24 inches, and can be added to pots as well as planted in drifts through a flowerbed. In addition to the standard pink petals, there are varieties from white through to a deep ruby red, and Dutch Grown stocks a good nerine selection. While it's too late to plant the bulbs this year, you can pre-order ready for planting in spring for floral fireworks next fall.

Sources indicate that another favorite is hardy cyclamen, which you'll likely find potted at your local garden center in fall. Plant a mix of the hardy ivy-leaved cyclamen (Cyclamen hederifolium), which flowers in fall and has pretty foliage that lasts through winter, and winter-flowering cyclamen (Cyclamen coum) which blooms winter into spring, for a long season of interest.

Recent findings suggest that even during the cooler months of the year, your outdoor space should be an inviting spot where you want to linger. A fire pit creates an ambient spot to gather around at dusk offers the opportunity for year-round entertaining, and is a go-to for landscape designers interested in creating an outdoor space with year-round usability.

In a recent development, whether you want the crackle of real wood burning or the convenience of starting a fire with the click of a button, a fire pit will add visual as well as physical warmth to your fall and winter garden. Opt for a design that complements your overall aesthetic and add layers of textured cushions and throws in a palette of warm, earthy tones to garden furniture to build on the cozy vibe.

Sources indicate that this fire pit is perfect for patio evenings, bringing friends and family together around a warm, inviting flame. Though it burns real wood, an airflow system facilitates efficient combustion to reduce smoke levels.

Fuelled by wood or wood pellets, this 7-inch diameter stainless steel mini fire pit brings the s'mores experience to a patio table. Efficient burning means it's smokeless and a removable ash pan makes clean-up easy.

It has been revealed that fuelled by propane gas, this stylish fire pit has an adjustable flame and can deliver plenty of warmth to keep your outdoor gatherings cozy. A lid lets it double as a coffee table and it's also available in black and stone-look.

According to recent reports, landscape designers often use a mix of materials to maximize texture and interest in garden design. These are automatically thrown into the spotlight during the cooler months of the year when plants die back and leave the hardscaping exposed. Gravel offers a softer alternative to bare paving slabs, and buff-toned pea gravel in mixed sizes and shapes like this landscaping pea gravel from Lowe's creates a particularly natural look.

Sources indicate that softening the edges of hard landscaping with plants is another landscape-designer trick that comes into its own as a garden moves from fall into winter. Use evergreen creeping thyme to blend the edges of a curving pathway and a functional garden element becomes an attractive winter feature. You can also use gravel as a mulch to avoid areas of bare border soil in winter, an option that's also easy on the budget.

Another way to maximise texture and help your garden transition from fall into winter without missing a beat is to add warm lighting from a low angle. In fall, a ground-stake spotlight will highlight foliage but then is easily moved to throw a glow through ornamental grass blades. Even a wash of light across a gravel path creates a play of shadows that highlights off texture to the full, and allows you to appreciate your garden from indoors on dark evenings.

In a recent development, the easiest way to create individual pools of low light is with solar spotlights, although you'll need to shop smart when buying outdoor solar lights that will generate enough power in fall and winter. For a start, choose lights with adjustable solar panels so they can be angled to match the sun's lower position in the sky. Look for a high conversion rate and a large capacity battery of at least 1500 mAh, too, and opt for warm-toned LEDS that will create more ambiance than bright white lights. These Solar Spot Lights from Wayfair tick all three boxes.

Industry observers note that lifestyle journalist Sarah Wilson writes about garden design and landscaping trends. She has studied introductory garden and landscape design, and also has an RHS Level 2 qualification in the Principles of Plant Growth and Development. She is a regular contributor to Homes & Gardens and Livingetc. She has also written for Country Living, Country Homes & Interiors, and Modern Gardens magazines.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

Dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with. Barking for no reason. The leash pulling that turns a simple walk into a tug-of-war. Turning the most expensive thing in the room into a chew toyâ¦.

Most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits. But the truth is, there is often a reason behind these irritating habits. Dogs communicate through behavior, and what looks like a nuisance is sometimes a symptom of an unmet need. The trouble is that we often get distracted by tackling that symptom when we really need to dig deeper.

Understanding what is driving an annoying or unwanted behavior can make it much easier to address.

In a recent development, dogs bark for many reasons, including boredom, anxiety, fear, a perceived threat, or a desire for attention. Any dog can develop a barking habit, regardless of size.

The key is identifying what triggers it. Boredom-related barking may improve with more exercise and mental stimulation, while anxiety or fear-based barking generally requires a more structured approach. Teaching a reliable "quiet" command and avoiding accidentally rewarding attention-seeking barking can also help.

Sources indicate that naturally vigilant dogs that spend their days standing guard at windows and alerting you to every passerby or suspicious-looking trash can may become less anxious if you block or obscure their view of the street. Limiting access to front-facing rooms or applying privacy film to windows can be a simple solution â if they canât see it, they stop worrying about it.

Chewing is normal for dogs, particularly teething puppies, but it becomes a problem when furniture, clothing, carpets, or walls become the preferred targets.

It has been revealed that boredom and anxiety can contribute to destructive chewing, as can a lack of appropriate outlets. Keeping suitable chew toys available, putting valuable items out of reach, and managing the environment while the dog learns what is acceptable can help redirect the habit.

In a recent development, A dog that greets visitors by launching itself at them has usually learned that jumping gets a response. Even pushing the dog away or telling it to stop can give them the attention theyâre seeking.

Recent findings suggest that ignoring the jumping and rewarding calm, four-paws-on-the-floor behavior teaches the dog that staying down gets the better response. Giving the dog an alternative behavior, such as sitting, can make the lesson clearer.

When faced with a friendly jumping dog, try the following:.

Keep your arms crossed, mouth closed, and eyes averted.

Turn your back, and walk away if they keep jumping.

Ignore them until they are calm and ready to listen to your command.

Dogs beg because it has worked before. Even one successful attempt at getting food from the table can establish the habit, making it particularly difficult to break.

In a recent development, feeding the dog before your mealtimes can reduce the motivation to beg, while teaching it to settle in a designated spot gives it something else to do. The biggest challenge is consistency. Giving in occasionally can keep the behavior going.

Table scraps can also pose health risks because some common human foods are harmful to dogs, while regular extras can contribute to obesity.

Recent findings suggest that leash pulling can make an otherwise enjoyable walk exhausting. Dogs often pull because they are excited and have not learned that pulling does not make the walk happen faster.

Loose-leash training takes patience. Stopping whenever the leash becomes tight and continuing only when it becomes slack teaches the dog what behavior allows the walk to continue. Rewarding the dog for walking beside the handler can reinforce the lesson, while a well-fitted harness may provide additional control during training.

Different dogs need different equipment, and what works for a small dog is not necessarily going to be suitable for a large one. Talk to your vet about the safest and most effective option for you and your dog.

Poor recall is frustrating, but it can also be dangerous if your dog runs towards traffic or another dog.

According to recent reports, training should start in areas with few distractions before gradually becoming more challenging. High-value rewards can make coming back more appealing, while using the recall command for unpleasant situations can create a negative association that undermines the training.

Sources indicate that digging is instinctive for many dogs and can also be linked to boredom or excess energy. Trying to eliminate the behavior completely may not be the most practical approach; redirection has a much higher chance of success.

Recent findings suggest that create a designated digging area, such as a sandbox or corner of the yard, making sure there is a clear distinction between this and the rest of the garden. It may be unsightly, but laying down some temporary netting or a similar obstacle in the rest of the yard can help teach your dog where they can and cannot dig. Burying toys or treats there can make the spot more appealing, while increasing daily activity may reduce the urge to dig elsewhere.

Some dogs struggle when left alone. The resulting distress can include destructive behavior, excessive barking, and other difficult behaviors.

Gradually getting a dog used to being alone, starting with very short absences and slowly increasing them, is an evidence-based approach. Providing a comfortable, safe space can also help.

Sources indicate that avoid making a fuss of your dog when leaving the house or on your return â your comings and goings should become part of an ordinary day, not an event. More severe cases of separation anxiety may require veterinary input or help from a behaviorist.

Aggression can have many possible causes, including fear, poor socialization, pain, territorial behavior, or negative past experiences. Because the appropriate response depends on the cause, this is one behavior where professional help is particularly important.

Sources indicate that A veterinary examination can help rule out an underlying medical problem, including pain. A qualified trainer or behaviorist can then help address the behavior using approaches such as positive reinforcement, desensitization, and counterconditioning. Punishment can make aggression worse rather than better.

Occasional accidents can happen, but frequent or sudden indoor elimination deserves attention.

Sources indicate that for dogs that are still learning, regular bathroom breaks and immediate positive reinforcement for going outside provide the foundation for housetraining. Enzymatic cleaners are useful for removing waste odors that can otherwise encourage a dog to return to the same spot.

If a previously house-trained dog suddenly begins having accidents, a check-up at the vet is appropriate to check for a possible medical cause.

Barking, chewing, jumping, digging, and the other behaviors on this list may be frustrating, but they rarely happen without a reason. Looking at what a dog is trying to communicate can reveal whether it needs more activity, clearer training, or a different kind of attention.

Addressing the underlying matter rather than simply trying to stop the behavior can make the problem easier to manage and help strengthen the relationship between you and your dog.

She built a miniature wheelchair using cardboard, tape, zip ties, wooden rulers, and Hot Wheels toy cars. The first version needed adjustments, but Mallory kept working until the little device was ready to support Gelato as he moved around. While this is certainly quite a unique solution, what isnât unusual is the compassion and creativity behind it. Help arrived in the form of an engineer who created a custom 3D-printed wheelchair designed to fit his body and accommodate his growth. The toy cars were gone, but Gelatoâs future mobility was looking more stable.

As the story of Gelatoâs unusual mode of transport spread, drawing plenty of social media attention, it also caught the eye of Hope Hollandsworth, a 28-year-old tattoo artist and devoted cat parent. When she first saw a photograph of Gelato during the summer, she felt immediately drawn to him.

Hollandsworth already cared for two cats with spinal injuries, Bread Crumb and Sprinkles. Both have limited use of their hind legs and rely on their front legs for mobility. Hope wasted no time, adopting Gelato as soon as she met him at the shelter. The five-month-old kitten spent his first night in his new home sleeping in her arms.

Industry observers note that absolutely. A disability does not automatically mean that a cat has a poor quality of life. Cats with mobility challenges can still enjoy affection, play, exploration, food puzzles, comfortable naps, and the tech giant of people they trust.

What really matters is understanding the individual cat's needs and making reasonable adjustments to help them live comfortably.

For a cat with a spinal injury, this may include providing easy access to food, water, resting areas, and litter boxes. Non-slip flooring, ramps, and thoughtfully arranged furniture can also help some cats move around more safely. Depending on the injury, a cat may need help with bladder or bowel function, regular skin checks, or a rehabilitation proposal.

It has been revealed that these are not small details. Some cats with spinal injuries cannot empty their bladders normally, which can lead to serious complications without very devoted care. A veterinarian can assess bladder function, mobility, sensation, and other concerns, then explain what support the cat will need at home. The real challenge is finding someone with the time and patience to take over these responsibilities on a daily basis.

Hollandsworth's experience with Bread Crumb and Sprinkles gave her a head start.

That moment is what inspired me to start Ariana's Doggos. Because when a dog has spent months living in a kennel, the version of them you see through the bars isn't necessarily their true self.

It has been revealed that dogs have always grounded me. They bring joy, companionship, and a sense of home, often asking for nothing in return. I started Arianaâs Doggos because I believe every shelter dog deserves to be seen for their potential, not just as an animal waiting behind bars. Recent findings suggest that what does this dog look like walking through a park? Do they love sniffing trails? Do they want to chase a toy around a pet store? Are they goofy? Are they cuddly? Do they want to say hello to every person they meet?

It has been revealed that before Ariana's Doggos, I worked in fundraising, media, and storytelling. I wanted to create something deeply visual and emotionally impactful.

At the same time, I became increasingly interested in rescue dogs and saw firsthand how the stress of a long shelter stay can affect them. I knew some rescues already gave dogs opportunities to leave the facility for walks or special outings, but I kept thinking about what could happen if those experiences became continuous storiesâthe difference between someone scrolling past a static photo and stopping to think, "Maybe that's my dog.".

Sources indicate that ariana's Doggos started as a personal media passion project about two years ago, based in Calgary, Alberta. This year, I've begun turning it into a more structured community initiative involving shelters, local businesses, sponsors, and people who simply want to see these dogs get a little more attention.

Something key to understand about shelter dogs is that a kennel is an extremely specific, highly stressful environment. A dog may be overwhelmed, overstimulated, shut down, or frustrated by everything happening around them. Rightfully so â they don't understand why they're there.

Shelter staff and volunteers who care for these animals daily see glimpses of their true nature, but an adopter on the other side of the kennel door rarely sees beyond the first impression.

In a recent development, A dog sitting quietly in a corner or barking like mad can be easy to overlook. That same dog walking beside you through a park, stopping to sniff a tree, looking up at you with a goofy expression, or happily carrying around a new toy tells an entirely different story.

And sometimes that story is what gets them noticed.

As rewarding as the outings are, there is also a side of this work that breaks my heart.

The first time you take a dog out, they can be absolutely ecstatic. Everything is new. They're sniffing, exploring, and soaking everything in.

It has been revealed that but when a dog has been waiting for a home for a long time, that excitement can start to change. They seem to understand the routine now. We're going somewhere, we're going to have fun, and eventually, we're going back to the kennel.

It has been revealed that that's also why I believe so strongly in the importance of foster homes and other individualized resources for long-stay dogs. Foster homes are an amazing temporary solution for many dogs, but foster networks are always limited, and more dogs will always be waiting for the right foster environment or a spot to open up.

Not every dog has an immediate foster match; some need a very specific environment, routine, or space. When those resources aren't available, dogs can remain in shelters for months. And the longer they wait, the easier it can be for people to overlook them. That's exactly why I keep showing up with a camera and a leash â every video is one more chance for the right person to finally notice them.

Recent findings suggest that right now, my focus is simple: one dog at a time. Taking shelter dogs out, creating meaningful experiences and exposure for them, and turning those adventures into story-driven videos that reach people far beyond the shelter walls.

According to recent reports, with Ariana's Doggos, the outing doesn't end when the dog goes back. The digital story keeps working long after the day is over, putting dogs in front of potential adopters.

I also have a bigger, long-term dream. Eventually, I would love to build a dedicated, foster-scale facility that could work alongside existing shelters and foster networks.

It has been revealed that it wouldn't replace shelters or traditional foster homes. Instead, I envision it as a centralized resource for shelter dogs who need extra exposure to find a home, basic training to help them fit into the right home, or a more individualized setting for dogs struggling with the shelter environment.

Most importantly, I want that environment to combine professional care with maximum public visibility through media and storytelling, preparing them fully for their future families.

In a recent development, I don't know exactly what Ariana's Doggos will look like years from now. Right now, I'm still building the foundation through these individual adventures and learning what works.

Every time I take a dog out, I'm reminded that these animals are so much more than their shelter profile.

They're goofy,  complicated, affectionate. They're curious and occasionally chaotic. They're individuals. They can become such an vital part of someone's life, and they deserve to be seen that way.

In a recent development, I may not be able to find a home for every shelter dog, but I can give them a day where they aren't a shelter dog. They're just a dog.

Sniffing a trail, choosing a toy, meeting a stranger, or getting the zoomies. A dog discovering something new.

And I can take those moments and put them in front of potential adopters who may never have looked twice at them in a kennel.

Because sometimes finding a dog a home starts with being seen.

Tech Report: What Your Hydrangeas Need in November – 5 Ways to Get Plants Winter-Ready and Kickstart Your Best Blooms Ever

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as November arrives, backyard activity may be slowing, but beneath the surface, hydrangeas are entering a critical transition.
  • Obviously, not all hydrangeas are the same.
  • Taking action this month gives you enormous benefits in the approach to the colder months ahead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as November arrives, backyard activity may be slowing, but beneath the surface, hydrangeas are entering a critical transition. As day length shortens and the air gets fresher and nippier, deciduous shrubs shift their energy into the roots. Understanding exactly what to do (and not do) for hydrangeas now begins with recognizing that dormant plants are still susceptible to moisture stress and sub-zero cold.

Obviously, not all hydrangeas are the same. Some form buds on old wood, which means pruning now is a no-no. Other types are hardier than others, and so need less winter protection. So in order to give hydrangeas the best winter care, you must first know exactly which type of hydrangea you have. However, these November care tips can all help to make a substantial difference to next year’s display.

Taking action this month gives you enormous benefits in the approach to the colder months ahead. Taking time now can help you shield key dormant buds from bitter cold, adjust water levels, stabilize and protect roots, and ensure your plants emerge stronger than ever next spring. So don’t chance it and leave your favorite shrubs unattended this month. Here are the crucial tasks to do before winter….

Effective fall care lies primarily in knowing your hydrangea type and variety. Varieties that bloom on old wood, such as bigleaf hydrangea (H. macrophylla) and oakleaf hydrangea (H. quercifolia) have already formed embryonic flower buds. If these buds freeze or are pruned off, next year's blooms will be tragically lost before you see them. Conversely, panicles (H. paniculata) and smooth hydrangeas (H. arborescens) produce flowers on new wood grown in spring, making them more resilient to frosts.

Sources indicate that popular bigleaf cultivars such as Nikko Blue or the Cityline series and serrated mountain hydrangeas need bud protection in cold zones. Cold-hardy panicle varieties like Limelight or Bobo and native smooth hydrangeas like Annabelle rarely require insulation, though they still benefit from consistent root hydration.

November hydrangea care also depends on your location, climate and USDA hardiness zone. Gardeners in northern zones 3-5 experience frozen ground and drying winter winds, demanding comprehensive stem barriers and thick thermal mulches. In contrast, those in southern zones 7-9 must contend with erratic temperature swings, where unseasonal late-fall warm spells can trick dormant buds into opening prematurely, only to be sheared by subsequent frosts.

Soil type also matters. Heavy clay soils hold water and risk winter ice pockets around roots, while light, sandy soils drain rapidly and dry out under frozen winds. Before tackling these tasks, it’s worth investing in a soil diagnostic tool with a long probe. The XLUX Deep Soil Moisture Meter, available from Amazon, gives instant readings to make better decisions before the first hard freeze. Don’t forget your trusty bypass pruners to remove any dead or damaged branches safely, plus some isopropyl alcohol to clean blades before and after use. You’re then ready to start….

One of the kindest things you can do for your hydrangeas this month is to “think twice, cut once” when it comes to pruning. One of the biggest hydrangea mistakes is indiscriminately shearing back during fall cleanups. For old-wood bloomers like bigleaf, mountain, and oakleaf varieties, the buds that produce next summer’s flowers are already set near the tips of the stems. Pruning these in November removes those flower buds, reducing or eliminating next summer's blooms.

It has been revealed that for these hydrangeas, you need to resist all structural shaping, topping, or cutting back until immediately after flowering finishes next year. The only exception is removing dead, diseased, or broken stems, which can be cut down to the base at any time. Use sharp bypass pruners like the Felco 2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon, for exceptional clean cuts.

Sources indicate that equally important is leaving the faded, papery flower heads all winter long. While it might be tempting to tidy up dried flower clusters on varieties like Endless Summer or PeeGee, these old blooms act as shields for the tender buds tucked beneath them. So it’s a good idea to leave them in place now. Dried flower clusters also add visual interest to the winter garden, especially when they collect small mounds of snow. Then, in late winter or early spring, as fresh green growth emerges at the base, you can snip the old flower heads off above the first set of green buds.

Hydrangeas need plenty of water, even now. While deciduous foliage yellows and drops, hydrangea roots take up moisture until the soil drops below freezing. Winter air and winds can be drying, and with the ground frozen, the roots cannot replace what gets lost. So don’t be tempted to put your hoses and watering cans away too early. Entering winter in dehydrated soil can lead to brittle branches and dead tips by spring. Get your hydrangeas as hydrated as possible before winter really begins.

It has been revealed that if you’re having a rainy fall, you might not need to water hydrangeas, but check the soil and give your hydrangeas a good soaking as needed. If rainfall is sparse, provide a deep, slow soaking every 10-14 days. Aim to moisten the soil 8-12 inches (10-15cm) deep, encouraging roots to settle deeper underground. Prioritize any newly planted shrubs, which need more water as they get established.

According to recent reports, soaker hoses are great options for targeted and controlled watering. You can buy Expert Gardener 50ft Soaker Hoses from Walmart to help you direct the flow wherever you grow your hydrangeas. Stop supplemental watering once morning frosts result in frozen soil.

Soil temperatures fluctuate erratically during late fall and early winter. Rapid freeze-and-thaw cycles cause frost heave, where expanding and contracting soil pushes shallow root crowns above the soil line, exposing roots to drying winds and freezing cold air. You can give key hydrangeas a helping hand by giving them extra insulation this month. This stabilizes soil temperatures, preserves deep moisture, and protects delicate roots through winter.

Start by adding a top-dressing of compost This will slowly break down over winter, releasing micronutrients that enhance soil and slowly feed the roots. A great composting option at this time of year is mushroom compost. You can get lush ready-made bags of Espoma Natural Mushroom Blend Fertilizer, from Walmart, to prime the earth and provide steady support through the colder months.

The compost can do double duty as an insulating mulch, but you can also use other types of mulch, like shredded bark or chopped leaves. Add a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of coarse, loose mulch. I like Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon, to help lock in late-season soil moisture and regulate soil temperature. Always leave a 2-inch (5cm) gap around the woody stems to reduce the risks of fungal rot and gnawing rodents.

If you’re in zones 4-6 growing bigleaf or oakleaf hydrangeas, sub-zero cold and winter winds pose a significant threat to next year's blooms. As noted, old wood hydrangeas have flower buds now. While the roots may be hardy to zone 5, flower buds can suffer frostbite below 0°F (-18°C). If stems die back, old-wood varieties will produce foliage during the summer, but zero flowers. So depending on your hardiness zones, consider adding some physical protection if your winters are very cold.

Do this in late November, after the plant drops its leaves and enters dormancy. Drive four sturdy hardwood or metal stakes into the ground around your hydrangea. Keep them several inches clear of the branches. Then wrap breathable fabric around the outside of the stakes to make a wind barrier. Use burlap or jute, such as Wellco Gardening Burlap Roll from The Home Depot, to protect against biting winds while maintaining healthy air flow around the plant. Secure with zip ties or twine.

For extreme northern climates, you can construct a cylinder of wire fencing around the plant and loosely fill with dry pine needles or oak leaves. Just avoid packing the leaves tightly and never use plastic tarps, which trap condensation and bake tender stems on sunnier winter afternoons.

Hydrangeas in outdoor pots, ceramic planters, and decorative troughs require proactive winter care. Unlike in-ground plants, potted roots are exposed to freezing air on all sides. An unprotected container's soil temperature can be 20°F lower than the garden soil, putting roots at risk of freezing and killing the plant outright. Ceramic and terracotta pots also absorb water, making them susceptible to cracking when wet soil freezes and expands. So you’ll need to give your container-based hydrangeas more protection if you have very cold winters.

In a recent development, begin by grouping potted hydrangeas together along a sheltered, south or east-facing foundation wall, out of wind corridors. Elevate your pots off cold concrete using pot feet or bricks to ensure drainage holes remain clear. Wrap the body of each pot in bubble wrap, thermal burlap, or foam insulation, securing the wrap beneath the outer rim without covering the top soil. You can also pick up floating plant jackets or anti-frost fleece covers, such as the Valibe Shrub Protection Plant Jacket from Amazon, which you can slip over potted hydrangeas in cold snaps.

In a recent development, if you are in zone 6 or colder, move your potted hydrangeas into an unheated garage, garden shed, or cold frame for the winter. These sheltered spaces keep plants dormant while protecting them from sub-zero drafts. Check on them once a month, providing a splash of water so the roots never completely dry out.

According to recent reports, as well as the things you should be doing this month, preparing your hydrangeas for the colder months requires knowing what to avoid. We’ve touched on pruning certain hydrangea types. Avoid aggressive pruning on old-wood varieties like bigleaf and oakleaf hydrangeas, which shears away next summer's flower buds. Another thing to avoid doing is allowing roots to dry out prior to ground freeze, as desiccated roots are vulnerable. Keep watering if the soil is dry and remains unfrozen.

Never apply high-nitrogen fertilizers at this time of year. Feeding now forces a flush of soft, tender growth that cannot harden off before freezing weather strikes, causing stem dieback. Don’t use clear plastic sheeting or non-breathable tarps as winter wraps, as they trap humidity, promote mold, and create greenhouse heat spikes on sunny days. This can trick dormant buds into waking prematurely. Finally, don’t just assume all hydrangeas need the same winter protection. Know your hydrangea type, how far north it is hardy, and how far you need to intervene to keep yours healthy.

Industry observers note that taking a little time in November to protect your hydrangeas makes all the difference for the year ahead. By maintaining hydration, shielding exposed old-wood buds from freezing gales, and insulating roots with a mulch blanket, you give your prized shrubs the exact winter protection they need. Come spring, your hydrangeas will emerge from dormancy strong, healthy, and ready to produce a summer display of blooms.

Hunger Games Fans, Did You Spot These 12 Hidden Plant Meanings in Sunrise on the Reaping?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there's something about Suzanne Collins' iconic dystopian series that feels more relevant than ever, and, with the latest film taking us back to the 50th Hunger Games, there's plenty for fans to scrutinize beyond the action itself.
  • If you've followed the franchise, you'll know that nature has never been merely decorative in Panem.
  • There's also a long literary tradition of using plants as an act of resistance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there's something about Suzanne Collins' iconic dystopian series that feels more relevant than ever, and, with the latest film taking us back to the 50th Hunger Games, there's plenty for fans to scrutinize beyond the action itself. Personally, though, I can't stop looking at the plants.

If you've followed the franchise, you'll know that nature has never been merely decorative in Panem. From sinister plants and poisonous berries to the natural world providing food, healing plants, and shelter, knowing your botany in the arena can quite literally mean the difference between life and death.

There's also a long literary tradition of using plants as an act of resistance. After all, flowers have carried hidden messages for centuries, from the symbolism of roses in mythology to the elaborate Victorian language of flowers, when a carefully chosen bouquet could communicate everything from secret affection to heartbreak.

Watch The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Trailer:.

A post shared by The Hunger Games (@thehungergames).

Even the names of some of the franchise's most memorable characters have botanical connections. Katniss is named after Sagittaria latifolia, a real North American aquatic plant also known as a swamp potato thanks to its edible tubers – making it a rather fitting namesake for a character whose survival instincts are so closely connected to the natural world.

Rue, meanwhile, shares her name with an aromatic herb traditionally associated with regret and sorrow (which is heartbreaking when you consider her story). And it seems the trailers and posters for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping suggest that the franchise's botanical language is far from finished.

From wildflowers carpeting the arena to carefully arranged floral displays around some of Panem's most recognisable characters, there are plenty of plants worth looking twice at in the posters and trailers alike.

Some have fascinating historical meanings, others have surprisingly sinister botanical properties, and more than a few might offer clues about the story's characters and themes.

With that in mind, then, here are 12 botanical details I've spotted – and what they could mean.

The striking urn plant, Aechmea fasciata, is a popular bromeliad that's hard to miss in the above Sunrise On The Reaping poster thanks to its architectural rosette of silvery-green leaves and bright pink flower spike.

Its name comes from the distinctive cup formed by its overlapping leaves, which collects water in its natural habitat. This adaptation helps the plant make the most of the resources around it, even when growing conditions are challenging.

In a recent development, it's easy to see why it makes an interesting symbol in the Hunger Games universe. Urn plants are associated with resilience, adaptation and protection – qualities that are essential when survival is the ultimate prize. There's something particularly fitting about a plant that creates its own little reservoir of resources in a world where nothing comes easily, right?

Get Ready For The New Hunger Games Film:.

Recent findings suggest that foxgloves (Digitalis purpurea) are among Britain's most recognisable wildflowers. Their tall flower spikes and bell-shaped blooms make them a favourite with pollinators and cottage garden enthusiasts... but there's a darker side to these pretty flowers. Every part of the foxglove plant is poisonous, containing compounds called cardiac glycosides that affect the heart.

According to recent reports, interestingly, those same compounds have played an important role in medicine. Digitalis-derived drugs have been used to treat certain heart conditions, making foxgloves a fascinating example of how the line between medicine and poison can depend on the dose.

In the Hunger Games, then, foxgloves could represent the duality of healing and danger – something that feels particularly at home in an arena where even the most beautiful things can be deadly.

White roses have long been associated with innocence, purity and remembrance. In Victorian flower dictionaries, their meanings included innocence, silence and even a holy death. Their appearance around President Snow is therefore particularly interesting, especially considering he's one of Panem's most ruthless figures.

Could they be a visual reminder of the innocence destroyed by the Capitol? Or perhaps a suggestion that even the most pristine-looking things can conceal something rotten underneath?

If white roses suggest purity, red roses are traditionally associated with passionate love and desire. They have been used for centuries as declarations of affection, but their symbolism isn't always straightforward. In the Victorian language of flowers, different shades and arrangements could carry different messages, from deep devotion to longing.

When red roses appear around President Snow, it's difficult not to consider the contrast between romantic passion and the bloodshed associated with his regime. After all, their vivid color also makes them an interesting counterpart to the white roses. Together, then, the two colors create a visual language of innocence, passion, power and mortality... which is very Hunger Games-coded.

It has been revealed that the California poppy (Eschscholzia californica) is instantly recognisable by its bright orange flowers. Native to western North America, it's also the official state flower of California. It's a hardy plant that thrives in sunny conditions and can tolerate relatively poor soils, making it a lovely symbol of resilience.

Poppies have different meanings across cultures, but they're frequently associated with remembrance, sleep and renewal. The California poppy's connection to the American landscape, though, makes it particularly interesting in the world of the Hunger Games, especially as it reimagines a future North America as Panem... especially as its bright and cheerful appearance feels so ironic against the darker world in which the Games take place.

Try the Burpee Sunset Mixed California Poppy Flower Seed from Walmart if you're in the mood for shades of orange, yellow, and cream in your own garden. You can even sow the seeds directly into gravel or cracks, too!

Industry observers note that if you've spotted the sunflowers in the character poster for Percy Daggs IV as Ampert, you're not alone in wondering what they mean for the latest Hunger Games film. After all, it's difficult to look at a sunflower (Helianthus annuus) without thinking of sunshine, happiness and optimism.

Recent findings suggest that these towering annuals are often associated with hope, loyalty and resilience. Their ability to grow quickly and produce impressive flower heads makes them a familiar symbol of strength and positivity, and there's also a lovely modern interpretation of sunflower symbolism that centers on community and supporting one another through difficult times.

Sources indicate that in a story where alliances can mean survival? Well, that sense of solidarity feels particularly poignant.

According to recent reports, canterbury bells (Campanula medium) are charming cottage garden flowers with tall stems covered in nodding bell-shaped blooms. And, fun fact, they're also the birth month biennial for May babies, too!

In a recent development, their traditional Victorian flower meaning was 'acknowledgement', while other historical dictionaries associated them more generally with constancy. And, in a story about loyalty, friendship and the people we stand alongside when times get difficult, both interpretations feel rather fitting.

Celebrate the Tributes' attempt to break the machine, then, with a packet of Canterbury Bells Double Mix from Amazon.

The unusual pincushion protea, from the genus Leucospermum, has an unmistakable appearance. Its spiky flower heads look almost like elaborate fireworks or, as the name suggests, a pincushion.

It has been revealed that native to southern Africa, these evergreen shrubs are adapted to challenging growing conditions and are known for their striking flowers. Proteas more broadly, though, have become associated with transformation, strength, courage and diversity. As such, their unusual appearance also makes them a natural symbol of individuality.

Their presence around Effie Trinket is a possible nod to her flamboyant personality, as Effie has always been someone who embraces color, extravagance and standing out from the crowd, even when the world around her is anything but cheerful. Peersonally, though, this writer thinks it might be a nod to her eventual character arc...

Toadstools might not technically be plants – they're fungi, as we made very clear in our recent piece on birth month mushrooms – but they deserve a place in this botanical spotter's guide.

Industry observers note that fungi are essential to healthy ecosystems, breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil. Some species, however, are highly poisonous, while others have medicinal or mind-altering properties, and that contrast gives mushrooms a fascinating symbolic role. They can represent decay and death, but also renewal, transformation and altered states of consciousness.

In the world of the Hunger Games, where the natural environment is often manipulated to confuse, frighten or kill its inhabitants? I suspect toadstools are a fitting reminder that not everything growing in the wild should be trusted.

It has been revealed that bee balm (Monarda) is a North American perennial loved by bees, butterflies and hummingbirds. Its colorful and nectar-rich flowers (particularly this stunning Pocahontas Purple Rose Bee Balm from Nature Hills) make it a wonderful addition to pollinator-friendly gardens, while the plant also has a history of traditional herbal use.

Recent findings suggest that today, bee balm is sometimes associated with compassion, empathy and comfort during difficult times. An RHS study of historical flower dictionaries, however, reveals that one nineteenth-century interpretation of this super-spreader was rather less affectionate: "Your whims are quite unbearable".

According to recent reports, that's quite a contrast to the modern associations of care and kindness – and makes its appearance in the sinister world of the Hunger Games all the more intriguing... especially for those who remember the role they played in the Sunrise On The Reaping book.

Now here's a botanical detail I particularly love, as Nepenthes is a genus of tropical carnivorous plants, commonly known as tropical pitcher plants. Their distinctive modified leaves form hanging pitchers filled with digestive fluid, which trap and break down insects and other small prey.

Industry observers note that the genus name has a fascinating origin. It comes from the Greek word nepenthes, associated with a mythical substance that banished sorrow or grief, which is an extraordinary name for a plant that catches and digests its victims.

In the context of the Hunger Games, the contrast is almost too good to ignore. A plant whose name evokes freedom from grief, but whose survival strategy involves trapping and consuming other creatures? Surely that's a dark metaphor for Panem itself (and almost worth buying a purple pitcher plant from the Ragnaroc Storein the run-up to the film, too).

A post shared by The Hunger Games (@thehungergames).

Recent findings suggest that spanish bluebells (Hyacinthoides hispanica) are popular spring-flowering bulbs, producing upright stems covered in clusters of blue, pink or white bell-shaped flowers. Unlike native blooms, though, these can spread vigorously in gardens and hybridize with native bluebells – something which hhis has raised concerns about the genetic integrity of native woodland populations.

In a recent development, the resulting hybrids can be difficult to identify, and experts advise gardeners living close to native bluebell populations to avoid planting Spanish bluebells. In terms of the Hunger Games, then, it's an interesting possible metaphor for displacement, hybridization and the arrival of an outsider that changes an established ecosystem.

In a story so concerned with power, territory and the destruction of existing communities, it feels like an idea well worth considering.

Beyond the individual plants seen across the posters and trailers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping, it's the wider meadow-like landscape of the arena that deserves attention.

Recent findings suggest that wildflowers are usually associated with freedom, biodiversity and the natural world growing without human interference, and tend to evoke a sense of peace and escape from the pressures of modern life. This arena, though, turns that idea on its head, forcing nature to become a part of the spectacle. Its beauty is carefully presented, but the environment is ultimately controlled by the Gamemakers. A field of flowers might look like an idyllic meadow, yet it exists within a space designed to test, manipulate and endanger the tributes.

It's a clever contrast between the natural world as something beautiful and life-giving, and nature as something that can be manipulated into a weapon. And perhaps that's the biggest botanical message of all: in Panem, you should never assume that anything is harmless. Even something as simple and innocuous as, say, a flower.

Waxing and waning signs, vague symptoms that come and go. A cat that is on deathâs door one moment, running around the next. Detecting illness in cats can be difficult enough, but when the body starts attacking itself, diagnosis becomes even more of a challenge.

It has been revealed that in an autoimmune disease, a catâs immune system malfunctions and begins attacking the body it is meant to protect. Fortunately, autoimmune disease is relatively uncommon in cats, but it can be serious and difficult to diagnose and treat. Because the signs tend to be vague and can come and go, they are easy to overlook, which makes it worth knowing what to watch for and when to involve a vet.

A healthy immune system protects the body from germs such as viruses and bacteria by sending out specialized cells to locate and destroy them. It also helps clear away damaged or diseased cells. These immune cells use protein signals on the surface of the bodyâs own cells to recognize them as safe. In autoimmune disease, a signaling error causes the immune system to treat the catâs own cells as a threat, and healthy, working tissue gets attacked and destroyed.

Industry observers note that cats can develop these problems much as people do. They can affect any part of the body, including the internal organs, blood, and skin, and there are many different types. Some can be life-threatening, weakening the bodyâs natural defenses while also damaging healthy tissue.

The part of the body under attack determines which signs appear, so the picture varies dramatically from one cat to the next. Signs are often general and not immediately linked to an autoimmune problem. Possible signs include lethargy, weakness, decreased appetite, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, and other changes to the feces. Other signs include pale gums, unexplained bleeding, bruising, a high temperature, a faster heart rate, rapid breathing, and tiring easily during play. Limping, swollen joints, sores on the skin, a poor coat, increased thirst, increased urination, and collapse are also on the list.

In a recent development, many of these signs come and go. A cat may seem completely fine one day and be struggling the next. Any of these signs are a reason to contact a vet promptly, since starting investigations early makes a real difference.

The problem starts with the catâs own immune system, which is part of what makes it so hard to manage. The exact triggers are not fully understood, and more research is needed. An immune-mediated condition can be triggered when the immune system is stimulated. Viral infections, vaccination, medications, inherited conditions, and hormones have all been linked to autoimmune disease. Where things get tricky is that the incident that triggered the disease is not usually the cause of the disease. That means that the same type of autoimmune disease can be triggered by different things in different individuals.

Some of these conditions can be passed down, and other possible contributors include poor nutrition, toxins, cancer, and stress. A cat diagnosed with an autoimmune disease considered hereditary should not be bred under any circumstances.

It has been revealed that diagnosis is often a process of elimination. More common causes of the same signs are investigated and ruled out first, which can mean lots of tests. A vet will start with a full physical exam and a detailed history, then choose tests to fit the signs. These may include blood and urine tests, X-rays, or an ultrasound scan. Samples may also be taken from wounds, rashes, or other affected areas. Prompt diagnosis is crucial for effective management.

In a recent development, treatment depends on the type of autoimmune disease, what part of the body is affected, and what is behind it, so it varies greatly. The usual approach is medication that calms the immune system so it stops attacking the body, most often corticosteroids like prednisone or dexamethasone. A large starting dose is often given, and once the signs settle down, the dose is lowered gradually.

Sometimes, stronger immunosuppressive drugs are also used. Some of them are also used in cancer treatment, and the side effects tend to be more severe. The trouble with treating an immune-mediated disease is that we are using medication to suppress the immune system, and that leaves the patient more susceptible to infection and other diseases.

Even more challenging when treating feline autoimmune disease is that some of the medications used to treat dogs or humans are toxic to cats.

In a recent development, supportive care matters just as much. Pain relief is often needed, but many commonly prescribed anti-inflammatory painkillers cannot be given alongside steroids. Stronger painkillers like opioids or gabapentin may be used to manage severe pain, and these come with their own side effects. Antibiotics may also be prescribed, either prophylactically if extremely high doses of immunosuppressive medications are being used, or if secondary infections develop.

For cats with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA), where the immune system is attacking and destroying red blood cells, or immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (IMTP) where platelets are being destroyed, blood or plasma transfusions may be needed to save a catâs life.

According to recent reports, lifestyle changes can help too. A cat with painful, swollen joints, for example, benefits from losing weight if overweight, and lower sides on litter trays and softer beds make life more comfortable. Each case is assessed individually.

According to recent reports, one of the more common autoimmune diseases in cats is known as Eosinophilic Granuloma Complex, a group of idiopathic conditions that are presently quite poorly understood. The exact cause of the disease is unknown; however, parasites, allergies, and genetic factors have been identified as likely triggers.

There are three main clinical presentations of eosinophilic granuloma complex:.

According to recent reports, ulcerative: Also known as indolent ulcers or rodent ulcers, this form of eosinophilic granuloma complex usually presents with a sore on the cat's mouth. It is typically seen on the upper lip. They are normally red in color and do not appear to cause your cat any pain or irritation.

Plaque-forming: often found on the stomach and on the inside of the hind legs. The lesions are often itchy and red and often become infected, which complicates matters.

Granuloma forming: usually presents as raised pink or yellow nodules that can be located anywhere on your cat.

Industry observers note that another more common feline immune-mediated disease is called pemphigus foliaceus. It affects the skin, causing scabs, crusts, and sores around the eyes and ears, on the paws, and in the groin area. When it develops on the paws, the nail beds can be affected as well.

There is no cure for autoimmune disease, but effective treatment and management can control the signs, greatly improve quality of life, and allow most cats to live fairly comfortably. These conditions can be debilitating and life-threatening, yet it is often possible to manage them well enough for cats to lead relatively normal lives. Because the signs overlap with so many other conditions, a vet visit at the first sign that something is wrong is the surest way to get answers early.

Got Fungus Gnats? This Easy Potato Trick Lures Hidden Larvae Out of Houseplant Soil

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You water your houseplant, and a little cloud of tiny black flies lifts off the soil.
  • Industry observers note that before you read up on how to get rid of fungus gnats, take a look at what's going on in the pot.
  • It has been revealed that one raw potato saves you the digging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You water your houseplant, and a little cloud of tiny black flies lifts off the soil. A minute later, they're on the window. Fungus gnats turn up in many homes once fall arrives, and they can hang around all winter. The next batch is already growing in the pot, and a fungus gnat potato trap is an easy way to find them.

Industry observers note that before you read up on how to get rid of fungus gnats, take a look at what's going on in the pot. The adult flies you keep swatting don't feed on your plants, but their larvae are a different story. Those live in the damp potting mix just under the surface, out of sight unless you go digging.

It has been revealed that one raw potato saves you the digging. Lay a slice on the soil, and the larvae come up to feed on it. Lift it a couple of days later, and whatever is in the pot is often feeding on the underside. Odds are there's a potato in the pantry already, so finding out costs you pretty much nothing, really.

A fungus gnat's whole life happens in or around the pot. They're small flies, often in the genus Bradysia, and a female can lay up to 200 eggs in damp potting mix. Once they hatch, the larvae eat for a couple of weeks and pupate near the surface, and fresh adults show up a week or so later. At room temperature, that's roughly three to four weeks per generation – so a few flies in October can be a lot more by the holidays.

According to recent reports, it's the larvae doing the eating. Their usual food is fungi and rotting organic matter, but they'll go after fine root hairs too. While a minor infestation won't usually do any harm, enough of them can damage roots and stunt growth, especially in seedlings and young plants. Watch for something like a tiny worm: clear or whitish, no legs, a shiny black head, ¼ inch (6 mm) long at most.

Cut a raw potato into slices about ¼ inch (6.4 mm) thick. Set one cut side down on the potting mix, and press it lightly so it sits flat. That contact is the whole trick. Larvae move up to the potato as a food source and gather on the moist underside where it touches the soil.

Recent findings suggest that give it a day or two before the first look. Flip the slice and check its underside, then the soil where it sat, for tiny clear larvae. Against dark, wet potting mix, they're hard to pick out, though, so a magnifying glass, like this Rongon 10X folding pocket magnifier from Amazon, helps a lot. Nothing there yet? Set it back down for another day or two. Sometimes larvae can take a few days to find the potato.

Recent findings suggest that don't leave it there for good, though. Raw potato breaks down in damp soil, and a rotting slice is just more of the decaying material larvae feed on. Toss the old one in the trash, larvae and all, and put down a fresh slice. Used like this, potato slices for fungus gnats let you track whether the numbers are dropping. Eggs won't show up on it. They don't feed, so they stay put in the mix.

So, do potatoes kill fungus gnats? Not really. The potato doesn't poison anything – it just draws feeding larvae up from the roots, and tossing a slice with larvae on it removes those ones. Eggs, pupae, and the adults flying around the room aren't affected.

According to recent reports, use the potato to check on things, then reach for something else to fix it. Say the slice comes up clean. That's nice, but it doesn't mean the pot's clear. Maybe there are only a few larvae, or they weren't feeding much. If flies keep hanging around, put down another slice.

Too much water keeps a lot of fungus gnat problems going. Short days and cool rooms slow houseplants down in fall and winter, so they use less water. Water like it's still July, and the mix stays wet, which eggs and larvae love. Let the top inch (2.5cm) dry before watering again. Empty the saucer, and make sure the pot drains. Old mix holds extra water as it breaks down. If a plant's due for repotting, look for a fresh mix with perlite for drainage, like the Back to the Roots Indoor Potting Mix, available from Walmart.

In a recent development, yellow sticky traps are for the adults. Push a few into the pot – you can buy sticky traps cheaply from Amazon. Each female stuck to one won't lay any more eggs, and the count tells you if things are improving. Down in the soil, the larvae aren't touched. If the gnats won't let up, try Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. israelensis), a naturally occurring soil bacterium. Despite the name, it isn't the Bt sprayed on caterpillars. This strain targets only fly larvae.

Summit Mosquito Bits use Bti to control both mosquito and fungus gnat larvae. Rather than scattering the granules on the soil, it's best to soak them in water for about 30 minutes, then apply that water to your houseplant soil. Repeat application about every five days, since Bti doesn't last long indoors.

Industry observers note that beneficial nematodes (Steinernema feltiae), such as BioLogic's Scanmask nematodes, are another organic option. These microscopic roundworms seek out fungus gnat larvae in potting soil. They enter the larvae and release bacteria that kill them, then feed and reproduce inside their bodies. It's pretty gruesome, but effective. They arrive alive in the mail, so use them right away. Keep the soil moist and the temperature between 60 and 90°Fahrenheit (16–32°C), or they won't work. Whichever you buy, check that the label allows indoor potted plants, then follow it.

Catching larvae early makes a fungus gnat problem much easier to control. A few larvae in one pot make for a far smaller job than a houseful of flies a month from now – and a potato slice is a cheap way to see whether your houseplant soil is hiding them.

So keep a potato around this winter. Set a fresh slice down whenever the flies show up again, and go easier on the watering while days are short. Fungus gnats have a much harder time of it once the top of the soil dries out between drinks!

Breaking: Why Your Houseplant Leaves Are Turning Yellow This November – and the Simple Fix to Reverse the Damage
