💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your houseplant leaves are turning yellow this November, your plant is sending urgent distress signals that you really need to heed.
  • Failing to adjust a watering routine in line with houseplants’ seasonal needs is the most common mistake we plant parents make, and unfortunately the root rot that results can be fatal.
  • So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your houseplant leaves are turning yellow this November, your plant is sending urgent distress signals that you really need to heed. As days shorten and sunlight becomes less intense in fall, most houseplants use far less moisture as their growth dramatically slows. Continuing your summer watering routine during this shift creates waterlogged soil, swiftly leading to root rot – and an avoidable trip to the compost bin. Catch that first yellow leaf early, however, and you can quickly reverse the damage to keep your houseplant happy and healthy.

Failing to adjust a watering routine in line with houseplants’ seasonal needs is the most common mistake we plant parents make, and unfortunately the root rot that results can be fatal. It takes a few weeks of waterlogged soil and rotting roots before the damage manifests with yellowing leaves, which is why this symptom usually shows up in November – and why once you spot a yellowing leaf you need to take swift action.

So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your houseplant with a yellowing leaf, and save it from an untimely death with a simple fix.

Take a closer look at the yellow houseplant leaf to see what tone, shape, position and extent of the discoloration is. Different plants show this early symptom of root rot in various ways: a Monstera will likely get a yellow halo on one of its monster-sized leaves while a ZZ plant leaf will turn bright yellow from top to bottom overnight. Peperomia foliage typically fades to a pale yellow while a snake plant leaf takes on a translucent yellow tone at the base. Matching up the symptoms to the plant species is a surefire way to tell if overwatering is the cause.

Match your houseplant to the symptoms and you have your diagnosis.

Large, thin-leafed tropical plants like monstera, calathea, anthurium and clumping philodendron typically show a bright yellow halo around a dark spot from overwatering. This happens because as roots begin to rot in soggy soil, fungal or bacterial pathogens in the potting mix travel up the plant and into the leaf tissue. Dead leaf cells show up as a black or brown area, and the bright ring of yellow around it is where the plant is attempting to stop the infection spreading.

ZZ plants (Zamioculcas zamiifolia), caladiums, and elephant ears (Alocasia and Colocasia) grow from potato-like rhizomes or tubers that store lots of water, so it can take these plants a little longer to show signs of overwatering. When they do, it's dramatic though! If these houseplants receive more water than they can process and rot sets in, nutrients are suddenly cut to a whole stem. The entire stalk and its foliage will quickly drain of color to turn a solid strong yellow, top to bottom.

Prayer plants (Maranta), peperomia, Chinese money plants (Pilea peperomioides), African violets (Saintpaulia), nerve plants (Fittonia) and Boston and maidenhair ferns all have a shallow network of very fine, fragile roots. Suffocating in overwatered soil, these thin roots rapidly disintegrate and the leaves lose their lustre then become limp and fade through pale green to a matte yellow. Don’t expect these leaves to be mushy from all that water: because the root damage cuts the water supply off, leaves will become dry and brittle, snapping off immediately when touched or simply dropping from the plant.

Recent findings suggest that jade plants (Crassula ovata), snake plants, Christmas or Thanksgiving cacti (Schlumbergera), echeverias and aloe vera all store water in their stems or leaves, and excess moisture causes them to turn a translucent, sickly yellow at the base. The area will also feel mushy and this may happen where stems or leaves meet the soil, in which case stems may topple over, but also where leaves attach to stems or leaf segments join together.

Recent findings suggest that vining plants like pothos (Epipremnum aureum), English ivy (Hedera helix), wax plants (Hoya) and heartleaf philodendron (Philodendron hederaceum) typically show overwatering symptoms on their oldest leaves near the base first. Unable to draw as many nutrients through suffocating roots, the plant strips nutrients from its older, less productive leaves to feed the fresh growth at its tips in the hope of finding a more suitable environment. Stripped of chlorophyll, the base foliage turns an even, uniform yellow while the newer growth at the stem tip remains green.

Recent findings suggest that overwatered houseplants with long, narrow leaves like spider plants (Chlorophytum comosum) and ponytail palms (Beaucarnea recurvata) typically develop brown foliage tips with a yellow area separating them from the healthy green tissue. This happens because the leaf tips are at the very end of the plant's plumbing system so, when roots are damaged and can't take up water effectively, are the first to run out of moisture. The yellow color below the dead brown leaf tissue is the plant trying to salvage what nutrients it can. The leaves may lose their upright arch and start to droop, too.

According to recent reports, if you spot yellowing houseplant leaves, immediately stop watering and let the soil dry out. Slide the pot off and if you see white roots, you’ve caught the problem in time. Pop the plant back into its pot and only water when the top inch of potting mix feels dry. A moisture meter like this from Amazon takes out the guesswork and helps you adjust your routine to the plant's fluctuating needs going forwards, and water houseplants properly.

If there’s a foul, stagnant smell, however faint, and roots look dark, root rot has set in and you’ll need to take action to save your plant. Remove as much soil as possible and use sharp scissors or pruners or to snip off all roots that look dark or feel mushy or slimy. Rinse the roots and wash the pot, then repot your houseplant.

Recent findings suggest that it's vital the pot has a drainage hole so excess moisture can escape (and a saucer to save your surfaces). If you adore a decorative hole-less pot, use it as a cachepot with a holed plastic pot inside. For succulent plants that store water in their leaves or stems, fill your pot with a fast-draining potting mix like Back to the Roots Organic Succulents & Cacti Mix, available from The Home Depot. For everything else, use an indoor potting mix with coconut coir and perlite that evens out moisture levels while allowing good drainage like Miracle-Gro Indoor Potting Mix For All Plants, available from Walmart.

Upgrade your irrigation with a watering can that has a long, gooseneck spout like this indoor can from Walmart for more precise, controlled water delivery.

Breaking: Why Tulip Fire Can Ruin Your Spring Flowers – And the 6 Simple Planting Steps that Help You Prevent It

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Planting some tulips is one of the most enjoyable ways to pass some time this month.
  • In a recent development, the frustrating reality of tulip fire is that while symptoms appear in spring, the infection usually begins months earlier during tulip planting.
  • Tulip fire is a common tulip disease caused by the fungal pathogen Botrytis tulipae.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Planting some tulips is one of the most enjoyable ways to pass some time this month. It offers the promise of vivid, saturated color to punctuate the winter months. Too often, however, the anticipation can turn to heartbreak, as early leaves emerge stunted, twisted, and scarred with spots. This is classic tulip fire: an aggressive fungal blight that leaves tulips looking as though they were scorched by an open flame.

In a recent development, the frustrating reality of tulip fire is that while symptoms appear in spring, the infection usually begins months earlier during tulip planting. The pathogen enters unnoticed on dry bulb scales, or lies dormant in beds where infected tulips grew before. Once established, no post-planting drench or spray can save infected stems. Your best defense is prevention before your tulip bulbs go in the ground. A few careful checks at planting time give next year's tulips a much better shot. Just a few proactive measures this fall will ensure that your tulips emerge clean, robust, and full of vibrant blooms. Here’s how to address the perils of tulip fire before it ever has a chance to cause problems – so you can look forward to spring with confidence.

Tulip fire is a common tulip disease caused by the fungal pathogen Botrytis tulipae. While closely related to common gray mold (B. cinerea), which attacks soft fruits and perennials, B. tulipae is host-specific and targets tulips almost exclusively. This host specificity is an advantage for gardeners. If you deny the fungus its preferred host for 3-4 seasons, resting populations in the soil gradually starve and decline.

Recognizing early symptoms is key to containment. In early spring, infected bulbs send up stunted, crumpled shoots known as fireheads. These sickly stems become blanketed in fuzzy gray fungal spores that blow or splash onto neighboring plants during cool, rainy weather. Tiny, water-soaked flecks quickly spread across foliage, coalescing into scorched brown blotches, while flower buds rot before opening. Wet spring conditions across USDA hardiness zones 3-8 accelerate spore dispersal, and can turn an isolated infection into an outbreak within a week.

It has been revealed that most cultivated tulip hybrids are at risk in damp, overcrowded conditions. However, species tulips with lower profiles (like Tulipa clusiana or T. tarda) and sturdy Darwin hybrid varieties demonstrate better resilience than dense, double-flowered late types. If you’re still deciding which bulbs to get, try bold Red Darwin Hybrid Tulip Bulbs from Amazon for weather resistant stems, and dreamily elegant Salmon Impression Darwin Hybrid Tulip Bulbs from Plant Addicts for natural vigor. Here's how to prevent your tulips turning into fireheads. Grab your bulbs and get ready!

Sources indicate that preventing tulip fire adds only a few minutes to your fall planting routine, but the benefits are immeasurable. Proactive defense focuses on basic cultural care: thoughtful checks, site and timing prep, and ample airflow. The following simple checks take just a little extra preparation, providing peace of mind and protecting your spring displays long before the first green shoots pierce the soil….

Recent findings suggest that before planting your bulbs, empty your bulb bags onto an outdoor potting bench or table, and inspect each one individually. A healthy, viable tulip bulb should feel solid, firm, and dense, with an intact papery outer tunic. Gently press the base plate and tip with your thumb. Any that give under your thumb, show mold, feel spongy, or have sunken yellow-brown patches should go in the trash.

Industry observers note that next, peel back a section of the papery tunic. Look carefully for sclerotia: tiny, hard, black or dark-brown resting bodies that resemble crushed pepper or poppy seeds. To help get a better look up close, the Jarlink 30X 60X Illuminated Jewelers Loupe, available from Amazon is equipped with bright LED illumination to check for those black sclerotia specks, as well as hidden scale lesions. These small sclerotia carry the tulip fire fungus between seasons. If you detect black specks or lesions, bag the bulb and throw it in the trash. Never toss diseased stock into home compost piles.

Resist the urge to plant your tulips while the ground is still warm. Botrytis tulipae fungal spores and resting sclerotia thrive in mild, damp soil conditions between 50°F and 65°F (10-18°C). Planting prematurely exposes bulbs to active soil-borne pathogens before the bulbs can establish robust roots. Delay your tulip planting until mid-to-late November or early December across most regions, after several hard overnight frosts have chilled the ground.

Soil temperatures should consistently measure below 50°F (10°C) at 6 inches (15cm). Cold soil suppresses fungal activity and forces dormant spores into inactivity. Planting after the first hard frosts is one of the most effective defenses against tulip fire. Even if an early frost hardens the surface, the soil beneath remains workable. Using a long-handled bulb planter like the Jardineer Bulb Transplanter from The Home Depot works well even in frost-encrusted fall soils.

Soil hygiene and thoughtful rotation are critical defenses against tulip fire. If your border suffered from tulip fire last spring, millions of sclerotia will have been shed into the earth as the leaves and flower petals decomposed. These resting bodies can survive in loam for 3-5 years, waiting to infect any latest tulips that push up through the contaminated soil, and start the cycle all over again. Give that bed at least 3 years without tulips, and plant new bulbs somewhere that's never had the disease. Fill affected borders with non-host species that tulip fire cannot infect, such as daffodils (narcissus), alliums, grape hyacinths (muscari), or crocuses.

In a recent development, if bed space is tight, containers are an easy workaround. Transition your tulips into patio containers. However, always dump out old potting soil, sanitize containers with a dilute vinegar or mild bleach wash, and plant in fresh, sterile soilless potting mix enriched with perlite. A lovely blend is Espoma Organic Potting Mix, available from Walmart, which is free of garden pathogens, and gives a low-release nutrient boost.

A bulb that sits in soggy ground all winter is in trouble, whether tulip fire shows up or not. Good drainage is critical. Tulip bulbs thrive in moisture, but can rot quickly in stagnant water. Planting in heavy, compacted clay or low-lying depressions also creates damp conditions where fungal spores multiply rapidly. Check your planting site a day or so after a soaking rain. Water that is still standing there, or dirt that balls up and sticks to your boots, means the spot would drain too slowly for tulips.

Sources indicate that select a planting site situated on high ground or a gentle slope. If you garden on heavy clay, avoid digging individual narrow holes. Instead, excavate the whole planting area 8-10 inches (20-30cm) deep. Blend some horticultural grit or coarse sand into the soil to help with drainage. Alternatively, for persistently soggy gardens, skip the fight and grow your tulips in containers or raised beds. You can get small bags of best-selling Miracle-Gro Perlite from The Home Depot for just a few dollars, and sprinkle a few handfuls into the planting site (or use it in your containers!).

Crowded planting designs may look lush in magazine spreads, but tightly packed bulbs create stagnant, humid conditions. After a few years, offsets and daughter bulbs fill in a bit more each season, and after a while the leaves will crowd each other. If tulips are jammed together, leaves that touch will stay wet longer after rain or a heavy dew, and spores won't have far to go to get from one plant to the next.

Give your tulips room to breathe by spacing bulbs 4-6 inches (10-15cm) apart in all directions. Make sure the planting site is not jammed against a fence or the side of the house. Choose open, sunny sites with steady airflow. Use jute twine like Vivifying Natural Jute from Amazon looped around some wooden stakes to help mark your plantings. Also, if you are naturalizing tulips in mixed borders, lift and divide dense perennial clumps every few years before planting your bulbs.

Old tulip leaves don't just vanish when they're left on the soil. On plants that were sick, fresh sclerotia form on the dying tissue and drop into the bed, and they can stay there until tulips come up through that ground again. Infected leaves, decaying stem bases, and dropped flower petals all produce fresh sclerotia as they wither. Left untouched, it decomposes into the topsoil, recharging the fungal spore bank.

Sources indicate that before planting new bulbs, do a fall cleanup. Rake through your beds and clear out old leaves, spent stems, and decayed organic matter. Pull back mulch to inspect the soil, discarding any dried plant remnants and flower parts from the previous growing season. Make sure you bag these remnants instead of composting them. You can buy best-selling Fabulas Yard Waste Bags from Walmart in triple packs.

Recent findings suggest that in spring, you need to stay proactive. Deadhead any spent flowers off suspect plants before their petals drop onto lower foliage, and clear out leaves and stems from anything that shows symptoms. Dig up any twisted firehead shoots, including the bulbs and adjacent soil. Do this the moment symptoms appear to keep airborne spores from spreading. Cleanup won't necessarily promise a clean bed, but it ensures there's a lot less fungus left behind to start the next round.

Recent findings suggest that once tulip fire takes hold in an established bed, it is one of the most persistent and frustrating bulb diseases to eradicate. So this fall care routine is massively beneficial in helping to break the fungal life cycle before it can cause damage. Take the right steps now when planting, and then you just have to wait for those first green shoots and a vibrant, spotless tulip display in spring.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success highlights that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Look, I'm calling it: the Bradford pear has had its moment. For years, its blooms have been everywhere, but now its the turn of an even prettier native tree to take its spot – and it definitely helps that it's a triple threat when it comes to blossoms, berries, and beautiful fall foliage!

I know, I know; it's a massive claim, especially as so many people rate the Bradford pear for its frothy white flowers, not to mention the pretty show its leaves put on when fall arrives. Still, there's a less attractive side to Bradford pears – and I'm not just talking about the unpleasant stench its flowers put out.

That's right, folks! As well as being notoriously unpleasant-smelling, the Bradford pear's branches are prone to splitting, and these trees can contribute to the spread of invasive Callery pears, too. So, if you're thinking about planting a fresh ornamental tree, it might be time to consider a more wildlife-friendly alternative.

My suggested swap for the invasive Bradford pear? Why, the serviceberry, of course!

This beautiful native tree pretty much does it all; think plenty of springtime charm in the form of beautiful blossoms, followed by delicious berries, and wrapped up nicely with some gorgeous fall foliage. And unlike Bradford pear, it's a valuable addition to a garden that welcomes local wildlife.

It has been revealed that serviceberry, also known as juneberry or shadbush, belongs to the Amelanchier genus. Depending on the species and variety, it can grow as a large shrub or a small tree, making it a useful option for gardens where a full-sized shade tree would be too much.

It is one of those plants that gives back much more than it takes, providing an early source of nectar and pollen for pollinators, sweet edible berries that work brilliantly in pies, jams and other homemade treats (although birds love them, too), and gorgeous fall foliage that promises to paint your yard in shades of yellow, orange and red before winter arrives.

In a recent development, all that from one relatively compact native tree? You'd better believe it!

One of the things I love most about serviceberry (as if all of the above weren't reason enough to be a fan!) is that most species grow well in full sun or partial shade, making it more accessible to people with all sorts of gardens. Just be sure to pop it in a spot with well-draining soil, as they won't appreciate sitting in waterlogged ground.

According to recent reports, for many homeowners, this native tree is a no-brainer, because what do you mean it offers the spring flowers that made Bradford pear so popular, along with edible fruit, beautiful fall color and valuable food for wildlife? Tick, tick, tick, and tick!

While it won't necessarily grow as rapidly or have the same uniform, upright shape as a Bradford pear, I think that's part of its appeal. And, with the world changing as quickly as it is, I think we can all agree that a garden tree should do more than look pretty for a few weeks each year.

A native beauty that gives back to local critters and puts out fruit that taste every bit as good as blueberries, then? Sign me up!

When my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

Itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

Any suggestions on what I could try?â.

You have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

Industry observers note that I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

Sources indicate that please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

According to recent reports, I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical issues sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we all adore the richly-colored, ruffled petals of peonies but if you’ve only got one plant in your garden, the show’s over in little more than a week. Plant some peony-like tulip bulbs, however, and you can enjoy months of very similar-looking flowers from early April all through May and sometimes even into June. These double tulips couldn’t be easier to grow, and this month is the exact right time to plant the bulbs.

Most tulips have six petals but a natural genetic hiccup capitalized upon by plant breeders means that some cultivars can have up to 50 packed into a single bloom. They’re known as double tulips, and their petal-explosion flowers look remarkably similar to peony blooms. Typically hardy in zones 3-8, they’re some of the best tulip varieties to kickstart spring in your garden, and the most striking spring-flowering bulbs to plant in November.

Sources indicate that the trick to enjoying months of flowers is to pick a pair of tulip varieties, one that opens early and one that blooms a little later. Early-flowering double tulips (officially known as peony-like tulips) begin blooming early in April. These tend to have shorter, sturdy 12-16 inch-high stems so stand up well to spring storms. Their tight layers of petals protect the flower core from cold weather, too, so each bloom can last for around 3 weeks – far longer than a standard tulip.

Late-flowering double tulips (known as peony-flowered tulips) bloom late April through May and are even more spectacular with huge flower heads on taller 16-24 inch-high stems. Because they're so top-heavy, these are more vulnerable to toppling in strong winds so in an exposed garden, give them a sheltered spot.

So, if you love peony flowers and you're wondering what to plant in November, look no further. Part of the Weekend Wins series, planting double tulips that look like peonies is one of those easy garden jobs that brings a big reward.

It has been revealed that when shopping for double tulips, it's key that bulbs are significant enough to fuel all those petals so early in the year, so always buy from a quality supplier. All our recommendations are for 10 bulbs.

‘Lorenzo’ gets spring off to a cheery start with long-lasting blooms in a luminous apricot-orange softly edged in creamy yellow, all through April.

With enormous blooms opening in late April and peaking through May, ‘Gudoshnik Double' has painterly petals streaked in yellow, orange and red.

A few double tulips are fragranced, and 'Avant Garde’ opens its buds in early April to release a sweet, floral perfume with beautifully fresh undertones.

In late April, ‘Pistache’ brings more creamy-white petals, this time splashed with wine red, and a wonderful scent of almonds and pistachios into May.

‘Foxy Foxtrot’ wakes up early in April, opening a lovely lemon yellow then gaining rich, warm tones of apricot, salmon-pink and honeyed gold.

In mid-to-late April, ‘Amazing Grace’ starts in a soft lavender pink with green accents, then shade-shifts into a deep rose tone that lasts deep into May.

In early April, ‘Royal Acres’ blooms open into bowls of intensely-colored, velvety magenta petals, often with a silvery sheen along the ruffled edges.

‘Dream Touch’ takes over the show from late April through May with enormous purple blooms, their striking petals prettily edged in white.

Though officially classified as a late tulip, ‘Mariage’ blooms in mid-April with deeply ruffled flowers in the prettiest pale rose-pink, and lasts into May.

‘Wild Romance’ adds creamy white petals with blushing pink picotee edges from late April through May, opening to reveal dramatic jet-black stamens.

‘Marshmallow’ opens in early April with a splash of bi-colored raspberry pink and ivory white petals, with a few green streaks for good measure.

Keeping the drama going, ‘Black Hero’, blooms from late April through May with ruffles of velvety deep-maroon petals that have a super sheen.

Growing spectacular double tulip flowers from fall-planted bulbs couldn’t be easier, and November is the exact right time to get them in the ground.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if there is one piece of decor that represents the holidays, it’s got to be a Christmas tree. Add an evergreen tree to your living room, toss on some tinsel, and, suddenly, it’s the holidays.

Industry observers note that but Christmas trees seem more expensive every year, and it’s not fun to spend all that money on a one-use tree that you'll discard in January. This is the year to switch to a beautiful live Christmas tree that lasts for years. There are lots of miniature Christmas-type trees that can be grown in pots, spruced up for the holiday, then enjoyed in the garden for the rest of the year.

Sources indicate that the key is to buy a living tree that is attractive and built for the long haul, not a single use. I’ve got you covered on that score with a short list of the best living Christmas tree options, from miniature traditional-looking spruces to unusual blue and golden conifers.

What’s the best small evergreen tree to grow in a pot for Christmas? Well, the answer will be different for each of us. There are plenty of attractive trees that make good live Christmas trees through December, then live happily in the garden the rest of the year. Pick your favorite, but make sure it’s suited to your USDA hardiness zone so it can thrive outdoors for years to come!

In a recent development, dwarf Alberta spruce (Picea glauca 'Conica') makes wonderful live, potted Christmas trees. These trees offer a classic pyramidal Christmas tree shape and incredible longevity – to 50 years or more in the right conditions. Their compact, densely packed growth habit makes these trees look cute, and they grow very slowly – between 2 and 4 inches (2.5–5 cm) per year – and top out at just over 10 feet (3 m) tall and wide. The needles are fine-textured and soft to the touch, a rich blue-green. They are also aromatic when rubbed.

You can order a classic dwarf Alberta spruce online at Nature Hills, or for something a little different, the Rainbow's End cultivar, which produces a second flush of lemon-yellow growth in summer.

These little spruces are easy to care for, drought-tolerant, and cold-tolerant. They grow best in well-drained acidic soil and prefer full sun. Only water when the top 3 inches of soil are dry. Their preferred climate (USDA zones 2–8) has cold winters and cool summers.

A dwarf blue spruce (Picea pungens 'Globosa') can make a great compact, living Christmas tree. You can doll it up for the holidays indoors, then move this slow-growing evergreen conifer outdoors for the winter in USDA zones 2–8. It needs little maintenance and offers a tidy, manageable size and striking silver-blue foliage.

The signature blue needles make the dwarf spruce a unique holiday tree, and its strong, stiff branches hold up heavy ornaments without issue. The natural pyramidal form requires little shaping, and its needles rarely fall out. On the other hand, the needles are prickly and can hurt you when you are decorating if you aren’t careful. Plus, this spruce doesn’t offer the beloved evergreen aroma, but a distinct odor that isn’t universally loved.

Dwarf blue spruce trees require very little attention once established. When you are moving the tree outside, put it in a site with lots of direct sun. Add several inches of organic mulch to the soil. The ‘Globosa’ cultivar, available from Woodies Garden Goods, reaches 3 to 5 feet (1–1.5 m) tall and wide.

It has been revealed that korean fir (Abies koreana) is a compact, slow-growing, symmetrical evergreen tree. With its soft, rounded needles and dense growth habit, it is a popular choice for a live Christmas tree.

It has been revealed that the needles are very ornamental, a dark green with a silvery underside, and offer a rich, fresh forest scent with notes of citrus. The cones are special too, a striking violet-purple and stand upright. This slow-growing fir creeps up a bit every year to finish at some 15-30 feet tall, with a conical form. A species tree will grow to 30 feet (10 m) tall, but a dwarf variety like Cis Dwarf Korean Fir, from Nature Hills, stops at 2 to 3 feet tall and wide. For something different, Ice Breaker Korean Fir is a dwarf variety that looks perpetually snow-covered.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, acidic soil. These trees thrive in USDA zones 5–7.

Recent findings suggest that A dwarf Norway spruce (Picea abies) makes a charming, compact live Christmas tree that can be kept in a pot or, in zones 3–7, planted in the garden after the holidays. These small trees typically reach around 3 feet (1 m) tall and wide at maturity, depending on the cultivar. They make charming, sustainable live Christmas trees and can be moved outdoors after the festive season.

Sources indicate that A dwarf Norway spruce tree offers a classic triangular shape, dark green needles, and graceful, drooping branchlets. This classic Christmas tree is popular for its dense, symmetrical shape and rich "Christmassy" scent that swiftly fills up the room. Unfortunately, Norway spruce needles can dry out and drop fast in warm indoor temperatures, so keep it in as cool a spot as possible.

Industry observers note that these trees are generally about 3 feet tall (90 cm) when sold as potted Christmas trees, and the ultimate height depends on the cultivar. They grow slowly, adding between 1 and 3 inches (5–10 cm) every year.

Industry observers note that you can buy both ‘Pumila’ dwarf Norway spruce and ‘Pusch’ dwarf Norway spruce at Nature Hills. ‘Pumila’ has a dense, bushy shape that looks lovely decorated for Christmas, while ‘Pusch’ offers something a little different, producing tiny red cones in spring that add extra interest to the garden.

Recent findings suggest that japanese cedars (Cryptomeria japonica) make unique live Christmas trees with soft, fine foliage that is pleasant to touch. The appearance depends on the cultivar, but many compact cultivars offer a naturally dense, rounded shape. The foliage can take on bronze, copper, or bluish-green tones during winter.

For a real statement tree, Black Dragon Japanese cedar, available from Plant Addicts, has a mature height of 8–10 feet (2.5–3 m), or for a smaller tree, the Tansu Dwarf Japanese cedar, from Nature Hills, reaches 3–4 feet (1–1.2 m).

Caring for your live Japanese cedar tree isn't difficult, but you’ll want to limit how much time it spends indoors. Too much time in a warm house can make the tree unhappy. Indoors, keep the tree away from direct heat sources. When it’s time to take the tree outside, start it out in a sheltered spot or an unheated garage for a few days.

Recent findings suggest that be sure to keep the soil moist. Check it every day. Japanese cedars thrive in full sun to partial shade in USDA zones 5–9 and require well-drained, fertile soil. Standard varieties can grow to 50 feet (15 m) tall if planted in the ground. Dwarf cultivars stay much smaller.

Industry observers note that you will recognize the lemon cypress (Cupressus macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’) – it’s the potted evergreen that you are likely to see in every store just before Christmas as a holiday plant. You can even get one from Walmart. It makes a charming, small Christmas tree with its natural pyramid shape, bright chartreuse foliage, and fresh citrus scent.

Sources indicate that the lemon cypress is a versatile evergreen that, once the festive season is done, can be kept in a container on a patio in USDA zones 7–10. Be gentle with it indoors. Use lightweight ornaments since the soft branches can bend or break under heavier decorations. You’ll want to avoid hot lights, too. Use battery-operated micro fairy lights that don’t produce excess heat.

In a recent development, these trees grow slowly and can top out at 10 feet (3 m) tall and 3 feet (1 m) wide. Indoors, give them a sunny window with 6 hours of bright light a day. Keep the tree far from hot air vents and cool drafts, and provide a pebble tray for humidity. Transition the cypress to an outdoor location after the holidays.

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

According to recent reports, that is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is currently looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

It has been revealed that rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

The interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

It has been revealed that the Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

It has been revealed that lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

It has been revealed that living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

Industry observers note that the current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:.

Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation.

Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment.

Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

It has been revealed that for families who decide to participate, it is important to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

When it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

In a recent development, the recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

There's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a significant deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

But this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

Recent findings suggest that aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

The Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

Itâs vital to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

When it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

It has been revealed that and anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

Recent findings suggest that that's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

Industry observers note that for owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, figuring out when to water houseplants seems like an easy call, right up until you're standing over a pot with the watering can. The top of the mix looks pale and dusty. You stick a finger in; it's dry, so you water. Then, a week or two later, the lower leaves go yellow, and it turns out the soil underneath was damp the whole time.

Too much water is behind a lot of the trouble people run into when watering houseplants, and fall makes it easier to get it wrong. Days are shorter now, and the light is weaker, so growth slows down, and a pot can stay wet far longer than it did back in July. Roots sitting in soggy mix can't get the air they need – and that's how rot gets started.

In a recent development, your finger only reaches the first inch or so. In a deeper pot, that top layer can dry out days before the root zone does. One fix is a moisture meter, like the Yamron 4-in-1 from Amazon. They're not expensive and offer an accurate assessment of soil moisture. But another way of checking is to use a wooden chopstick – it costs nothing, if there's one left over from takeout in a drawer somewhere, and it reaches right down to where the roots are.

Bare wood soaks up moisture. Push an untreated chopstick or bamboo skewer down into damp potting mix, and the wood darkens wherever it touches wet soil, and crumbs of mix stick to it when you pull it out. Dry mix behaves differently. Dry particles just fall away, and the stick comes back pale and mostly clean.

Sources indicate that have you ever done the toothpick test on a cake? It's the same idea, just backward. With a cake you want the toothpick clean, but in a pot, a clean chopstick means the mix has dried out at that depth.

One crucial point: you must use plain wood for this. Lacquered or painted chopsticks shed water, so they won't darken much. A plastic one only highlights you whatever soil happens to cling to it, and not much else, honestly.

According to recent reports, grab a clean, dry stick first. Any leftover dampness from the last check will throw off the reading. Standard chopsticks are long enough for small and medium pots, but major floor plants sit in deeper containers, and that's where 12-inch bamboo skewers come in handy. Walmart sells a pack of 100 for a few dollars.

According to recent reports, push the stick in partway between the main stem and the rim, straight down into the root zone. Did it hit resistance on the way? Ease off and try another spot, because forcing it through a thick mass of roots can damage them. Then leave it there, alone, for about 30 seconds to a minute so the wood has time to pick up any moisture.

In a recent development, slide it out slowly and look along the whole length. If there's a dark band near the bottom with mix stuck to it, the lower part of the pot is still wet – even if the top inch came out clean.

If you still can't make sense of the stick, use a soil moisture meter or a leave-in option, like the Sustee Aquameter, which sits in the pot full-time and fades from blue to white as the mix dries. Either way, the reading only tells you what's in the pot. What you do next depends on the plant.

A damp chopstick generally means there's still water down there, and a clean, dry one suggests the mix has dried out at the depth you tested. That isn't an automatic cue to grab the watering can, though. Peace lilies need their mix kept moist but never soggy, so water once the stick starts coming out dry through the upper part of the pot. Wait much longer, and the whole plant usually droops hard.

Industry observers note that pothos can go drier than that, a fair bit drier. Let the stick come out dry through a good share of the pot before you water. Snake plants and succulents go further still, and they're safest when the stick comes back clean all the way to the bottom. In winter, a snake plant may only need water every month or two. When one of them has been sitting in soggy mix for weeks, repot it into a fast-draining mix, like Miracle-Gro cactus, palm and citrus mix from Home Depot.

Chunky orchid bark is the significant one. Those chunks are too coarse to stick to wood, and the bark soaks up water inside each piece rather than holding it on the surface. You can pull a clean, dry-looking chopstick out of a pot that's still plenty moist. Gritty, very coarse mixes muddle things the same way. A badly rootbound plant is tricky too, just in a different way. There's hardly any mix left between the roots, the stick won't go in easily, and water poured on top can run straight down the sides and out the drainage holes.

Industry observers note that use the chopstick as one clue, then. It can't measure anything precisely, so back it up with a few other checks. Pick the pot up right after a good soak and again a few days later, and you'll learn how light it feels once it's dry. Check the leaves as well. Yellowing lower leaves on a heavy pot usually point to too much water. And make sure every pot drains freely. Clear nursery pots with drainage holes, like these from Walmart, let you see roots and dark, wet mix through the side.

Industry observers note that A calendar can't see inside a pot. If you water on the same day every week, it can go fine all summer and then start leaving roots wet for days once fall arrives and the light drops off.

Chopsticks are about as cheap as plant tools get, and one highlights what's happening under the surface while watering needs shift with the seasons. Keep a dry one next to the watering can. It'll be right there the next time the soil has you guessing.

Halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

Recent findings suggest that halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

Industry observers note that keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

Costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs important to pay attention to how they respond.

A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

Recent findings suggest that A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

In a recent development, there's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

According to recent reports, halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

It has been revealed that jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

Sources indicate that real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

Sources indicate that the liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

Recent findings suggest that check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

Recent findings suggest that handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

Closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

In a recent development, keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly notable on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

Recent findings suggest that if a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

Industry observers note that check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

Halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

Recent findings suggest that it's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

The 2-Minute Lard Trick That Helps Smaller Songbirds Get Their Fair Share of Food in Fall and Winter

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you're feeding garden birds this fall, you'll know that fat balls and suet feeders are often mobbed by dominant birds like starlings and grackles, leaving nothing for more timid feathered friends to feast upon – which is why you should also smear a little lard on a tree or fencepost.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're feeding garden birds this fall, you'll know that fat balls and suet feeders are often mobbed by dominant birds like starlings and grackles, leaving nothing for more timid feathered friends to feast upon – which is why you should also smear a little lard on a tree or fencepost. Adding fat to your bird feeding buffet is essential as temperatures fall, but small birds who need this energy-boost most often miss out. However, this quick bird-feeding trick ensures smaller, shyer nuthatches, chickadees, titmice, wrens and creepers get their fair share of high-energy fuel, because bigger birds are unable to cling to this vertical surface to feed.

It has been revealed that smearing lard, tallow or vegetable shortening onto a tree only takes two minutes4 but this simple addition really can make a difference to how smaller garden songbirds fare in winter. The smaller a bird is, the more vulnerable it is to freezing or starving as temperatures drop, and the more likely it is to be bullied from feeders by more aggressive birds. This fat-smear trick bypasses those bullying birds, mimicking natural foraging to tempt even cautious birds like brown creepers who are far too shy to use regular feeders.

In a recent development, if you like to feed birds in winter, tree-smeared lard can attract unusual visitors like woodpeckers to your yard as insects become scarce, and you'll also enjoy watching nuthatches walk headfirst down the tree trunk to enjoy their fat feast. Smearing lard on a tree also avoids the danger of smaller birds getting their tongues, claws or legs tangled in a fat-ball mesh holder. You can also easily mix birdseed into the fat to provide extra nutrients, or try our super-tasty bark butter recipe below.

Any tree or fencepost will do, but aim for a more mature tree or older fencepost that has furrows or cracks that will hold more lard and give clinging birds a foothold. Take a golf-ball sized chunk of lard, tallow or vegetable shortening and press it onto the wood, ideally 5-6 feet high, on the shady side of the tree or post so it doesn’t melt in the sun.

Recent findings suggest that mix in a pinch of cayenne pepper to deter squirrels if needs be, as they’ll quickly learn to leave it alone while birds are unaffected by the taste and heat. Only smear enough fat on the tree for birds to finish during daylight hours to avoid attracting nocturnal scavengers like racoons and opossums. And if you live in bear country, wait until late November or December when they're in full hibernation before trying this trick.

You can use animal-based lard or tallow, and plant-based vegetable shortening to feed garden birds in winter using this quick trick.

Lard is cheap, full of fast energy for birds and has a soft, buttery texture so is easily pressed into bark furrows. Look for a product that’s 100% pure lard such as South Chicago Packing Lard, available from Amazon. You’ll find similar products at most grocery stores but read the ingredients list carefully: while you don’t need to worry about citric acid, avoid synthetic stabilizers like propyl gallate, BHT or BHA, commonly added to grocery-store lard to prevent it going rancid. Don't use products with added salt or sodium as birds can't process it and high levels can be fatal.

Tallow is simply suet in rendered form and, again, you need to look for a product that’s 100% tallow such as Farmer Bob’s 100% Beef Tallow, available from Amazon. It has a similar consistency to lard and has a higher nutritional value as well as being a great source of energy.

It has been revealed that vegetable shortening is less nutritious but it still provides a valuable high-energy boost to small songbirds in cold conditions. For regular use, an organic all-vegetable shortening such as Spectrum Naturals Organic Shortening, available from Walmart is best. Unrefined and free of synthetic preservatives, it retains some nutrients and is firm enough to use for this trick. It's fine to use Crisco, also available from Walmart, if that’s what you already have in your panty, but it’s less nutritious and melts more easily so think of it as an occasional junk-food treat for birds.

Sources indicate that in the North, Midwest and Mountain West, temperatures are cold enough to simply smear lard or tallow straight onto the tree or post without it melting or spoiling in fall and winter. Vegetable shortening will need mixing with cornmeal to stiffen it up before using. Of course, you can still add ingredients to lard and tallow to increase the nutritional value.

In the South and Southwest, mild fall and winter days can be warm enough to soften lard, tallow and vegetable shortening, so mix with cornmeal to form a firmer dough before using.

In a recent development, while plain lard smeared onto a tree or fencepost works just fine, this no-cook recipe will tempt even the shyest feeders. Mixing a handful of natural, raw ingredients into the fat also creates a pliable dough that’s the perfect consistency to press into bark furrows in all zones.

It has been revealed that providing food for small, shy songbirds in this way is a useful part of a bird-food buffet in fall and winter. The more ways you can offer food, the better, from planting berried shrubs that provide a natural feast for winter birds to saving kitchen scraps for your feathered friends. Different species prefer different food types and also to feed in various ways, so using a range of bird feeders to satisfy different species is a smart move, too. Just don't forget to cater for the smallest backyard birds with this quick lard-smear trick.

At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

Industry observers note that some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

According to recent reports, when I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

Industry observers note that âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â.

Sources indicate that mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own crucial role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

According to recent reports, different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

In a recent development, that Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

During the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

When a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

The roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

In 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 new volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

Industry observers note that âSpicy loves me, and she is not happy when she sees me go into a different enclosure to pet another dog,â Mark said. âI have to do it in a way that I hide from her so she canât see or she won't stop barking.â.

It is a sweet story, but it also highlights why understanding each dog's personality matters.

In a recent development, hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how crucial volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She notes the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â.

According to recent reports, camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

In a recent development, three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how promptly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

Two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

According to recent reports, as for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her new home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

Industry observers note that âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â says Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â.

Some dogs find their people quickly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:.

âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â.

According to recent reports, the sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

In a recent development, at Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

Maybe that is what makes them lucky.

Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

And that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

And every morning, people arrive.

Someone opens an enclosure.Someone picks up a leash.Someone brings a treat.

And perhapsâ¦that is what makes these dogs lucky.

This should come as little surprise to those on top of their gardening trends, of course, because much of 2026 has come with a distinctly gothic twist – whether that's due to the gothic romance of Wuthering Heights, the bewitching gardens seen in Practical Magic 2, or Kat Von D's maximalist approach to black tulips.

It has been revealed that still, it's nice to see something a little different steal the spotlight from the world of pastel blooms, right? And Lilium 'Nightrider', the nearly black lily that's set to appeal to anyone who prefers their flowers with a little more drama, does exactly that.

It has been revealed that with its rich purple-black petals and subtle satin-like sheen, this striking lily looks almost completely black in certain light. It's an unusually dramatic color for a summer flower, giving it an almost otherworldly and deeply Wednesday-coded quality that's hard to ignore.

Of course, it's not just the color that makes 'Nightrider' so special, or the fact that its upward-facing blooms appear in clusters on tall stems, creating a striking focal point wherever it's planted.

It has been revealed that no, it's the fact that you don't need to be an expert gardener to enjoy this showstopper. Like other garden lilies, 'Nightrider' is relatively easy to grow, making it a really good choice for gardeners who want maximum visual impact without an overly complicated planting scheme.

Industry observers note that the trick is to do the opposite of what you'd do with Wednesday Addams herself: give it a suitable sunny or lightly shaded position. Then, top it off with well-drained soil, then sit back and wait for that striking show come summertime!

Shop Gothic Blooms That Wednesday Would Love:.

It goes without saying that this is a flower for those who love a little mystery, dramatic contrasts and planting that makes a statement, which is why you need to think hard about the flowers you pop it next to.

With that in mind, try pairing its almost-black blooms with silver foliage, deep burgundy flowers or soft white planting for a really striking combination that feels like something straight out of your favorite gothic romance.

According to recent reports, alternatively, leave it to do its Wednesday-style thing, and let it stand alone in a container where its unusual coloring can take all the attention. One thing is certain: if you're looking to introduce a little gothic glamor to your garden, this nearly black lily deserves a place on your radar.

I am confident in saying that a certain Miss Addams would absolutely approve.
